subtopic: SHIPMENT OF SYRUPS FROM WEST INDIES.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On. the Orders of the Day:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine) :
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: SHIPMENT OF SYRUPS FROM WEST INDIES.
speechtext:
The right hon. leader of the Opposition made inquiry of me yesterday with regard to the service being rendered by the line of steamers, subsidized by the Canadian Government, which run from St. John and Halifax to the West Indies and I told my hon. friend that I would endeavour to get the information for him.
The Royal Mail Steam Packet Company is the company that rune this line of steamers between Halifax and St. John and the West Indies. I asked the Deputy Minister of Trade and Commerce this morning to read my right hon. friend's remarks and mine in yesterday's Hansard and send me a statement with regard to the matter. I have the statement here in the form of a letter from Mr. O'Hara, the Deputy Minister :
Ottawa, Out., March 16, 1916. Dear Mr. Hazen:
X have read in Hansard of yesterday the remarks of the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier upon the subject of the shipment of syrups from the West Indies, and also your reply.
The information you gave to Sir Wilfrid is correct, but, in the absence of Sir George Foster I may add, that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has been aware for some time of the congestion existing in connection with the service of the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company to the West Indies. This congestion exists both ways. Neither Canadian exporters or importers are able to get the space they demand, and Sir
George has been doing everything he possibly could to relieve the situation, even to cabling the Admiralty to release some of the ships commandeered from the Royal Steam Packet Company, without success.
The company states that 70 per cent of their tonnage is now in the hands of the British Government. Canadian exporters of lumbe-, flour, and other foodstuffs have been complaining of the small amount of space available, as have complaints come from Canadian importers and West Indian exporters of their inability to get sufficient space for sugar and molasses.
The difficulties are heightened by reason of the fact that there are no tramp steamers available for the molasses trade, which steamers always largely divide the traffic with the Royal Mail Steam Packet steamers. The Royal Mall Steam Packet Company are giving the best service Canada has ever had to the West Indies. They are performing the service under subsidy, with the vessels required, and so far as we know are doing all they can with the space at their disposal to accommodate the shippers, at either end, to the capacity required.
I may say that the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company have ever shown a sincere desire to meet this department in every request we have made of them, even though such requests at times exceeded the limits of their contract.
Yours faithfully,
F. C. T. O'Hara,
Deputy Minister.
206th BATTALION-SUPPLY OF KITS.
On the Orders of the Day:

subtopic: SHIPMENT OF SYRUPS FROM WEST INDIES.
speechtext:
I .call the attention of the acting Minister of Militia to the following article which appears in this morning's Daily Mail of Montreal:
Made in Germany; Kits supplied to Local Battalion-Col. Pagnuelo expresses indignation over Kitts given the 26th Battalion.
Three hundred kit bags were received this week from the Department of Militia, Ottawa, for the men of the 296th French-Canadian Overseas Battalion, now being recruited by Lieut.-Col. T. Pagnuelo. Each kit was neatly packed and contained the usual soldier's toilet haberdashery, consisting of a military brush and comb, toothbrush, razor, service shirts, etc. But, to the surprise and disgust of the commanding officer, upon examining the articles it was found that many of them were marked. Made in Germany. " I was never more disgusted in my life," said Lt.-Col. Pagnuelo to a Daily Mail representative. " It is either another imposition of graft or the exercise of gross negligence on the part of the militia authorities in permitting unscrupulous manufacturers to unload German-made goods upon the Government, particularly for the use of Canadian soldiers. I only hope," added the colonel, " that my men will be given the opportunity of using these same razors on the despicable Hun, and it cannot be too soon to suit us."
Another prominent officer of high rank said that nothing could be more inconsistent in view of the present agitation to place a boycott on everything of German manufacture. " William the Brutal, by fair means or foul, and mostly foul, is out to place himself as conqueror of the world and as vice-regent of heaven," he said. " This is one way to help him to attain that end."



This paper is friendly to the Government, and I should like to know from the acting Minister of Militia if he can give us any information upon this matter, and what the Government intends to do.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
subtopic: SHIPMENT OF SYRUPS FROM WEST INDIES.
speechtext: It would certainly not be the intention of the Government to buy anything made in Germany at the present time, and perhaps that policy may be carried out after the war. All razors that have been purchased, so far as I know, have been purchased either in Great Britain or in the United States. There are no razors made in Canada. No razors of German origin have been purchased, so far as we know. I shall have the matter looked into, and try to give my hon. friend some satisfactory answer.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

I see in various newspapers a statement attributed to the Minister of Finance that certain financial arrangements have been made by the banks with regard to a credit for the money necessary to ensure further orders for munitions in Canada. Would the minister tell the House just what has been done?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In order to give my hon. friend and the House the information which he desires, it will be necessary for me to refer to a conference which I convened early in December last; I think during the first week of December. This was after the domestic war loan had been made. My hon. friends will recall that the domestic war loan was for a sum of $50,000,000, but that subscriptions were received aggregating over $100,000,000. It was before we had dealt with the matter of those subscriptions that I convened this meeting of representatives of Canadian bankers, in fact, of all the general managers of Canadian banks, for the purpose of taking up what then seemed to us to be a very important question by reason of prevailing exchange conditions, namely, the question of providing in Canada a credit for the Imperial Government for the purpose of paying for munitions and other supplies ordered in Canada.
It will not be necessary, unless my hon. friend especially desires me to do so, to refer to the exchange situation further than to state, as I have indicated, that the conditions were serious, and that it looked as if the Imperial Government, in the absence of such a credit, would not be able to place further orders for munitions, at least upon a large scale, in Canada. At that time the banks were engaged in the task, a very heavy task from the financial standpoint, of moving the western crop. After conferring with the bankers, I stated that, in view of the fact that the Canadian war loan had been made and would of course make demands upon the financial situation, and in view of the fact that further demands were being made upon the banks by the requirements of the crop movement, it appeared to me that public opinion would support the Government in allotting subscriptions to the amount of $100,000,000 of the domestic war loan. It was my view that we should take $50,000,000 for the purposes of our war expenditures, and that we
I

should set aside $50,000,000 as an Imperial credit here for the purpose of enabling the Imperial Government to finance the requirements of the Shell Committee or the Imperial Munitions Board in making its payments to manufacturers and others from time to time. My hon. friends in the House know that that policy was followed with very happy results, I think very happy [DOT] Imperial results, because the announcement was received most favourably both in Canada and in the United Kingdom.
I stated further to the bankers at that time that this credit would last for a few months longer, and that, in the spring, I would again convene them for the purpose of seeing whether it would not be possible on the improved financial situation which would then exist, to establish a further credit here, or to adopt some expedient, such as the establishment of what is called dollar exchange, for the purpose of facilitating payments here by the Imperial Government, and getting over the exchange difficulty which still continued serious.
In brief, I may say that we have had several conferences extending over the last two or three weeks, and the result, I was able to announce yesterday that the Canadian Bankers Association, representing the several banks of Canada, had made an offer which I am informed is entirely acceptable to the Imperial authorities to establish a credit of $75,000,000 for the Imperial treasury here. The result will be that any difficulties, so far, as financing in Canada is concerned-and when I speak of difficulties, I refer to exchange difficulties- have been overcome for some months at least, and that further orders will be placed in Canada, in due course, to the amount of at least $75,000,000, and, I am hopeful, to the amount of $100,000,000. In anticipation of the arrangement being concluded, because I have had information for some little time past, that it would likely be concluded, orders aggregating some $20,000,000 have already been received by the Imperial Munitions Board from the Imperial authorities.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

speakeroldname: Hon. T. W. CROTHERS (Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I desire to rise to a question of privilege. On the editorial page of yesterday's Toronto Globe appears the following:
When the Minister of Labour at Ottawa was reported as telling- the House of Commons that
" he was not sure Great Britain and her Allies would win the war," that " a German victory would mean a German Canada," that " he did not approve of everything done by the British House of Commons for the relief of disabled soldiers," and that " no one knows when this war will cease or how it will end," there was a general feeling of painful surprise. Mr. Croth-ers, having had abundant time allowed him for the correction of published reports, and having admittedly prolonged silence that he had nothing to plead in bar of condemnation, may fairly be held responsible for his peculiar point of view and mode of expression.
That is* the first statement of the kind which I have seen or heard since the occasion referred to. It is a gross misrepresentation of what I said, although perhaps about 'as near the truth as the Globe generally gets when dealing with the utterances of political opponents. This statement, referring to me, says, among other things:
He did not approve of everything done by the British House of Commons for the relief of disabled soldiers.
The intent being, apparently, to convey the idea that I was not in sympathy with disabled soldiers. That statement is entirely without foundation in fact, and is wholly fabricated. I made absolutely no reference in my remarks to the relief provided for disabled soldiers by the British House of Commons, as a reference to the unrevised edition of Hansard would clearly show. Concerning our own soldiers, I said, as appears on page 1709,' Hansard:
I was glad also to hear the remarks of the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), and the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) concerning the treatment which we should mete out to our returning soldiers.
Both hon. gentlemen spoke very sympathetically as to the men who might return from the front disabled or wounded, and took the position that we should leave nothing undone to enable them to secure an honourable livelihood, and to re-educate them if necessary; and, as will be noticed, I expressed my pleasure at the stand taken by those two hon. gentlemen from Oxford and Edmontoji respectively. I said:
I am very gl& d to know that every member of this House, and I believe every person in Canada, appreciates to the full the great sacrifices that our young men are making in fighting our battles on the fields of France and Flanders They are making the supreme sacrifice there. '
I pointed out that everything possible was being arranged for them on their return through the Military Hospitals Commission.
I said further:
We are not unmindful of the soldiers. Nothing is too good for the man who has risked his life for the British Empire.. . This commission

is composed of some of the leading men in Canada. They are giving their services. . . They are doing their very best for returned soldiers, and will continue to do so regardless of any adverse criticism.
I did not use the words attributed to me: " He was not sure Great Britain and her Allies would win the war." I was pointing out the necessity of our concentrating all our efforts towards the successful termination of the war, and among other things I said:
We are not, as some people say, feimply rushing to the assistance of the Mother Country, as, of course, we did, but that we are fighting for the liberties we enjoy as Canadians, which would be sacrificed if Germany should win.
Mr. Pugsley: I think we all agrde with you in that.	1
Mr. Crothers: I thought my hon. friend made some observations to the effect that he did not believe there was any danger in that direction.
The hon. member for St. John did not deny having said something to that effect, but he said:
Mr. Pugsley: I am sure we are going to win, that is all.
Mr. Crothers: I am not so sure.
The word " so " is left out of the Unrevised Edition. I said further:
No man knows when this war will cease, or how it will cease, and while we are in that position it seems to me we should concentrate all our efforts on the successful prosecution of the war, and not divert our strength therefrom in any way whatever.
These remarks were quite in accord with those made by Lloyd George, and many other prominent men in England on many occasions since the beginning of the war. 'The right hon. the leader of the Opposition ,on the 19th August, 1914, said in substance that there was danger at the front when he used the words:
We offer no criticism, and we shall offer no criticism so long as there is danger at the front.
Danger of what at the front? The danger now is no less than it was then, and in substance the right hon. gentleman said what I am criticised for saying, and it will now be in order for the Globe to instruct the right hon. gentleman's following in this House to depose him from the high and honourable position he now occupies. .
Some hon. MEMBERS : Oh, oh.

speechtext: I thought my hon. friend rose to explain, blit he is attacking.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I am trying to justify -what I said by what was said by my right hon. friend, for whom I have the highest respect.

On motion of Sir Thomas White (Minister of Finance) the House went into Committee -Mr Rhodes in the Chair-to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to authorize the G overnor in Council to raise by way of loan, in addition to the sums now remaining unborrowed and negotiable of the loans authorized by Parliament by any Act heretofore passed, such, sum or sums of money, not to exceed in the whole the sum of seventy-five million dollars, as may be required for paying maturing loans and obligations of Canada, carrying on of public works authorized by Parliament and meeting expenditures for general purposes authorized by Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The object of this resolution is to replenish the necessary borrowing powers of the Dominion for the purposes mentioned, the present borrowing powers being only about $10,000,000 due to our large borrowings of the past year. The Appropriation Act of 1915 recites that there remains unborrowed and negotiable of the loans authorized by Parliament, for the construction of public works and other general purposes, the sum of $78,291,206.04. I propose to file, for the information of the House, a statement showing that the balance which can be borrowed under the authority of that Act is at the present time $10,897,425.88.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What was the amount authorized last year by the statute?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Finance Department, -February 9, 1916.
The purpose of this resolution, as I have stated, is to replenish our borrowing powers which have become too low for our purposes. Hon. members will understand that financial conditions are unsettled and uncertain, and it is in the interest of the Dominion that we should be in a position to take advantage of favourable opportunities for borrowings as they arrive. I may state that last year the conditions, in their susceptibility to change, were almost kaleidoscopic, that a favourable opportunity would arise for a loan and that a week or ten days afterwards the conditions would be unfavourable. I think it is not necessary to enlarge upon that point. We are simply asking the House to enlarge, to the amount we deem sufficient, the present statutory borrowing powers of the Dominion Government. The House is doubtless aware that for several reasons it is inexpedient to borrow at present in the United Kingdom; if for no other reason the exchange situation, and the large cost of bringing money to'this country if borrowed there. We are therefore limited practically in our borrowings to this side of the Atlantic; in other words, to Canada and to the United States. I am going to ask the House, if it will be good enough to do so, to accelerate the passage of this Bill in order that it may have its third reading to-morrow.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Will this
$75,000,000 exhauist the amount which my hon. friend intends to borrow this year, or will he have to come back to the House again?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister will introduce, this year, as he did last year, a Bill to cover the estimated war expenditure of the Dominion for the coming year. My right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) will recall that the Prime Minister introduced a Bill authorizing an expenditure amounting to $100,000,000 last year. I am not quite certain as to the amount which will be asked for by the Prime Minister for that purpose for the coming fiscal year, but I
should think it would be in the neighbourhood of $250,000,000, as stated in my Budget speech. The Dominion, for the coming fiscal year, will be confronted, using round figures, with a situation in which, from April 1, 1916, to March 31, 1917, we shall have to raise by way of loans in the neighbourhood of possibly $200,000,000 or $225,000,000. I am unable, of course, to state the amount definitely because the sum will depend upon the number of men who will be und,er arms by the end of the year, and the times at which they enlist. We have the Canadian market, and we have the American market, but we borrow in Canada for war purposes. This $75,000,000 will be part of the entire borrowing which I have mentioned.	-
Is that the loan which is mentioned in the evening papers of to-day as being about to be completed by J. P. Morgan & Company?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For some weeks past negotiations have been proceeding, but they have not yet been concluded, between the Dominion Government and a New York group of financiers looking to the placing of a loan there.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I understood the Minister of Finance to say what we practicaly knew already, that the Prime Minister will introduce a Bill providing for the war expenditure. I understand that, according to the arrangement which has been made, this war expenditure will be provided for by the British Government, but what I want to know from my right hon. friend is, if this amount which my hon. friend asks the House for now is all that he intends to apply for and. to borrow, apart from what will be borrowed under the Bill to be introduced by the Prime Minister? -

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
ada, in the United Kingdom, and in France. We use a certain amount of that Imperial credit from month to month for the purpose of making our payments in the United Kingdom and in France, hut I d,o not de^ sire to draw upon it to a greater extent than is absolutely necessary because I should prefer that Canada should, as far as possible, pay her own way. Great Britain is labouring with unprecedented financial responsibilities.
While the Imperial Government is willing to give us this credit, should we desire to avail ourselves of it, it is the earnest wish of the Government that we should not avail ourselves of that credit to a greater extent than is indispensably necessary. Answering my hon. friend, then, in the light of what I have said,' this will not he the limit of our borrowing, apart from our borrowings from the Imperial Government during the coming fiscal year; at least, in my view it will not, because I think that our expenditures for war will be such that we shall have to provide a total in the neighbourhood of $200,000,000 or $225,000,000. We shall take advantage of the Imperial credit when we find it indispensably necessary to assist in our financing, and particularly in our financing in the United Kingdom and on the continent of Europe. In my view we shall require at a later date-many months from now, possibly towards the end of the year-to borrow further amounts, possibly in Canada. My hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) asked me the other day whether I had in mind a domestic loan. My hon. friend is aware that it is a good maxim not to state what you are 'going to do in the matter of borrowing. I am sure he will recognize what is an obvious fact, that it was really a wonderful achievement for Canada to subscribe $100,000,000 towards the loan last year, and to me it is a matter *of very great pride that notwithstanding the $100,000,000 which we took last year from the people's savings and from the financial institutions of Canada for the purposes of the war, the banks are now able to come forward and furnish an additional credit of $75,000,000. Now, that credit of $75,000,000 is a further reason why for the present at all events, it would in my judgment be inexpedient to bring on a domestic loan.

I do not want to hinder in any way the Minister of Finance in getting through this resolution, and the necessary legislation authorizing this loan. Three different financial propositions have been mentioned here to-day:

an advance to the British Government by Canadian banks; the loan now under consideration, and a war loan to be submitted later to the House. I have discussed this question on one or two occasions since the war began, and the only objection I have to the minister's proposal to-day is that to my mind it is not on a sufficiently large scale, and further, under the present circumstances, I think we should' adopt what I would call more modern methods of financing. I think we should re-organize our whole financial position. We should nationalize our currency to begin with, instead of having, as we now have, a bank currency. In the next place, we could adopt the system now in vogue in the United States, and in practically all other countries, of a national bank of re-discount. I believe that if we called on the New York market to-day -to my mind we should have done it before this-we could get a loan of $500,000,000 for the use of Canada, and we could get it better now, probably, than later on. We do not know what may happen in connection with the United Sstates market, and that is now the one available market for Canada. I should like to have seen the Finance Minister go to the New York market for a loan of $500,000,000, $250,000,000 of which could be paid to us in gold, and deposited in the treasury as a 25 per cent reserve against a possible issue of a billion dollars of national currency in case we should require that money in connection with this war. I believe that would have been a better way of financing under the present circumstances, and it would not have been over-straining the banks, as we may be doing now, in asking them and the Canadian people generally to finance Canada. At the, present time there is a super-abundance of capital in New York. To my mind we should proceed on very large lines, and when the opportune time arrives-and I believe it has arrived to-day-we ought to avail ourselves of it. I should like to have seen the Minister of Finance re-organizing the currency of this country.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: On what line?

I would withdraw from the banks the privilege they now have of issuing a bank currency, and in place of that I would allow them to draw on the national currency in practically the same proportion. I would let them have money at one per cent, and grade it up. That would give them the same resources they have to-day under the system of bank

currency, and it would enable us to establish a bank of re-diseount such as they have in the United States. I believe the Canadian banks would consent to be parties to a bank of re-discount very much on the line of the United States system. Practically every civilized country in the world to-day with the exception of Canada, has a national currency and a system of re-discounting. This method of financing is modem; it is sound; it has been justified by practice; and it gives a nation and a Government an elas-, ticity of credit, and affords greater facilities and larger credit to the business of the country. I am convinced that it is not only sound, but in the interests of the country. Some may say that I am proposing what may be called rag money, but I do not think a national currency backed up by a gold reserve of at least twenty-five per cent would be a dangerous, a soft, or an inflated currency. It would be a currency and a system of banking equal to the growing requirements of the country, and equal to war conditions as they are. To my mind, because of the dislocation caused by the war, we cannot, carry out the work of reorganization in Canada without an absolute reform in our system of financing. To do it right we must have a national currency. If we had that, Canada could help finance the Mother Country in her expenditures on munitions, and it would also bring us a lot of business.
We are moving along those lines now, but in a small, picayune way; we are asking the banks to finance a loan of $75,000,000 for the use of the Imperial Munitions Board to pay for orders for munitions. We should put that load, not on the banks, but on the credit of Canada as a nation and as a country having a line of credit, and if we had the courage to have a national currency and a bank of rediscount, we would, take a great load off our banks, and we would be able to finance not only our own country, but the Mother Country. Canada's credit to-day is equal, if not superior, to that of every other country in the world, and if to-day we offer a loan on the New York market for $500,000,000, the same amount as the Pranco-British loan, the Canadian loan would sell at a better price and at a lower rate of interest than did, the Franeo-British loan.
For what purpose would you borrow that $500,000,000?
For the purposes of Canada. That is the very point I am coming to.
Who would lend you money on such grounds?
Who would?
England was borrowing money to pay for supplies produced in the United States. What excuse would you give for borrowing $500,000,000?
I would borrow $250,000,000 as a 25 per cent reserve against a possible issue of national currency up to $1,000,000,000, if such, an issue became necessary.

What excuse
would you give?

I would give the same excuse as we are giving now in connection with the $75,000,000 which the Minister of Finance proposes to borrow, that is, for the general purposes of Canada. I am not going to give all the details of the proposal, but I am asking this House to finance on more modern methods and to use the national credit in order to have a national currency, and to lessen the weight on the banks and on our people by improving our banking system. The Minister of Finance speaks of the banks financing a loan of $75,000,000. I am told that orders for munitions of war to the extent of $1,000,000,000 would be placed in this country if they could be financed. Well, we are to have a loan of $75,000,000 now and the banks are to finance it. I do not quite knbw how they are to do that; I can only imagine, and perhaps my imagination is wrong in the matter; but it may be that t'he banks will be able to raise the money to pay for those munition orders that we have heard about by issuing a Canadian national currency against the deposit oi British bonds with the Minister of Finance. Such a scheme, if it could be carried out, would be all right; but it ought to be carried out on much broader lines. We ought to start with a national currency and the creation of the Bank of Canada, as I would call it, which would be a bank of rediscount and which would rediscount for all the banks of Canada any paper or any securities that they cared to deposit with it. In other words, the Bank of Canada would be an organization for
4 p.m. the emission of the national currency to the banks as they required it, on rules and regulations to be made by Parliament and by the Department of Finance, and it would also rediscount for the banks any securities that

they had to offer. In that way our banks would he largely relieved from the duty imposed upon them of financing Canada, not only for general purposes but for war purposes, and of helping to finance the Imperial Government in connection with the war.
My proposals may he radical, but I do not think they -are, because they have been carried out elsewhere; and in discussions which I have had with gentlemen who have been in America in connection with the financial situation in Europe and the financial requirements of Great Britain, I have been informed that the best way to assist in the finanacing of the Mother Country and of ourselves would be to have the courage to adopt these two modern systems of banking which I am advocating. We have them in skeleton form now, but we do not have them on our statute book as an essential and integral part of the financial organization of Canada. We are to-day rediscounting in a way for banks, and we are using the national currency in order to aid various proposals, but we are doing it in a roundabout fashion. We ought to do it in a broad way, and the time to do it is now if the opportunity has not already passed. We could, however, place a large loan on the New York market; we could use a portion of that loan as a gold reserve for the issue of a national currency, and in that way we could permit our banks to devote all their energies and all their credits to the reconstruction of Canada which must ensue after the war is ended. There are two duties resting on our shoulders at the present moment; the first is to carry on the war and help the Mother Country in every way; the second is to take care of Canada and to see that there is abundance of money for the reconstruction of the country, and the surest and fairest way of providing the necessary money is by an issue of national currency, and by having a bank of rediscount. As long as I am in a position to do so, I intend to present to the people of this country the fact that this practice, which has been the practice in other countries, is the proper method of financing in Canada.
There is a demand in the Canadian West for a system of farm credit, and the same demand is pressing from the other provinces. We must give our farmers a system of credit which will be an improvement on the present system. At the present time we are making petty amendments to the
til". W. F. Maclean ]
Banking Act allowing our banks to extend their practice ' in the making of loans to our farmers; but the way to get credit for the farmers of this country and to put money at a cheap rate at their disposal for the development of their farms, the purchase of livestock and things of that kind, is to have a system of farm credit based upon the credit of the nation. The proposal that has been put forward in the United States, and that will be passed in an amended form, is based largely on the authorization of the United States Government to deposit its moneys and its own currency with land	banks.
No currency in the world to-day is equal to the national currency of the United States. If we had here such an abundant national currency, based, as I have said, on the necessary gold reserve, we could make advances to these land banks by way of national currency, absolutely secured in every case by mortgage. We could create an investment security that would probably run at 4 or 5 per cent; that would give our farmers abundant money at a lower rate. If we reform our currency system and our financial and banking system now, in this time of war we shall finance ourselves better than we are now doing; we shall do more for the Mother Country than we are now doing. Besides, by taking this course, we would help the general business of the country, strengthen the Canadian banks, and assist the Canadian farmers. The only argument that I have ever heard against the suggestion I make now is that it would strike a blow at the hanks that now have a bank currency. I say it would not. Provision could be made whereby they would have just as liberal a currency as they have to-day; they would have to get it from the nation, and the nation would have security for it. We cannot succeed in business, competing with the United States, if we have not as good a banking system as they have. They are ahead of us in this respect; the reorganization that was effected within the last two or three years in the United States was the result of most careful inquiry by a commission appointed by Congress a good many years ago. After examining the history and methods of banking organizations all over the world, they came to certain conclusions, which have been embodied in the system now prevailing in the United States. They are carrying the system of re-discounting further now by providing an abundant credit for the farmer. I repeat that we shall not be able

do our duty by our own country or by the Mother Country until we have as good a banking and currency system as they have in the United States. That we recognize the value of their methods is proved by our imitating them, though only in a half-hearted way: we are rediscounting, through the "Minister of Finance, for the banks, but not as they do it in the United States. We are going to have some kind of system of farm credit for our farmers; I am glad to know that the minister has put himself on record in connection with that. To my mind, however, he has not come right up to the full opportunity that is before him, and I hope that he will widen his views in this respect, having regard to the enormous requirements of the country at the present time. We are only beginning to hear of these requirements. We have heard of two requirements of $75,000,000 to-day, an advance to the Mother Country for munitions, and a very large loan, in connection with which the Prime Minister is going to bring down legislation. Why not make a combination of the whole thing on the newest and most approved lines of banking and national finance? If he should do that, the minister would widen his reputation, improve the condition of affairs in Canada, and allow this country to be a still greater help to the Mother Country in the present hour of trial.

I do not rise with a view to obstructing the adoption of this resolution. I have some confidence in my hon. friend the Minister of Finance; I think he is a well-meaning Finance Minister, and if he were left to his own good self, the administration of the Finance Department would be carried out in a manner satisfactory to the Dominion at large. Unfortunately, he has been frequenting certain company of late, and I fear that in consequence he may become somewhat given to unwise expenditure. I observe that this money is to be applied to public works and to meeting expenditures for general purposes authorized by Parliament. I am not forgetting, in the crisis through which we are passing, that I represent a farming community, where a dollar is a dollar and a shilling a shilling, and where the people have learned the four rules of arithmetic. In view of the fact that so many loans are cropping up, one after the other, the time has come for the Government to curtail expenditure. I repeat what I said the other evening when I had the honour to address the House on the Budget: we should
have a round table conference, where the representatives of the two parties could unite in applying the pruning knife to the Estimates. While we are passing through this awful crisis, I think we can easily save to the country at least a quarter of a million dollars. The hon. member for South York is sailing under false colours. He is a radical with a false label. Interesting as his argument is for a change in the national currency, when tire Minister of Finance is proposing to borrow more money from the United States I should expect from the hon. member for South York another argument than the one that he has just offered to the committee. I would remind the hon. gentleman of a certain issue of the Toronto World, which appeared at a time preceding the elections of 19111. I remember that it was during the dog days-July, if I mistake not- and, as it was very hot, my hon. friend was represented as addressing an immense meeting on the outskirts of Toronto, not far from his own constituency, with his coat off. He was arguing against that awful reciprocity pact, and he was telling the electors of South York that the Canadian people should not truck or trade with the Yankees.
Never.

He was telling them that we should do nothing with the Yankees.
Mr. W, F. MACLEAN: Never.

To-day he has another
theme. He suggests a change in the national currency, but he has nothing to tell my hon. friend, who was one of the leaders of the noble eighteen in Toronto who attacked so vehemently the last Administration because, forsooth, a pact was made between the American Government and the Canadian Government by which there would be the right to exchange certain natural products between the two countries. Nobody was compelled, according to the Fielding-Knox pact, to do business with the Americans. The Canadian people were left perfectly free to sell or to -buy from the United States, but in the present instance, to my great horror, I find my hon. friend the Minister of Finance coming before this Parliament asking for legislation by which he will be authorized to borrow the sum of $7)5,000,000. It is not stated in the resolution that he will borrow it from the United States, on the New York market, but he has just stated in so many

words that he is not going to issue a domestic loan but that he is likely to get this money from the Americans in New York. I am simply shocked to hear my hon. friend, my honest friend, the Minister of Finance, coolly proposing that this Canadian Parliament should authorize him to borrow money from the Yankees. I am sorry that Old Man Ontario is not in the House to-day. I see many of the representatives from Ontario. What would they say if their electors were in this House to-day? Or what would their electors, think if they were here this afternoon and heard this discussion, and heard the Minister of Finance proposing that Canada should borrow $75,000,000 from those awful Yankees in' New York? We remember how one of the apostles of the 'Conservative party in the last election stated that with the Reciprocity Treaty the banking accounts of Canada would be transferred from Montreal, 'Toronto,, and Winnipeg, to Chicago and New York, and that Canada would become the 'backyard of the United States and we also remember
It was Taft who said that.

We remember what
scorn was expressed by hon. gentlemen when the Taft letter appeared in which mention was made of Canada becoming an adjunct of the United States. Well, Sir, for the second time this fiscal year, Canada is going, by her representative the Minister of Finance, on the New York market to borrow money from the Americans. When my hon. friend made his loan of $45,000,000, I noticed some very harsh criticism in the financial papers of the country because ot the way the loan had been underwritten in New York. It was said that the rate of interest was rather high for such a good security as the one offered by my hon. friend. It was stated that this loan would affect adversely other loans made by Provincial Governments or by municipalities in the Dominion. How is he going to underwrite this loan? Of course he may not think it wise to give the House the procedure he is going to follow, but, at all events, I think we should he made aware of this fact, whether or not tenders will be called or whether it is going to he underwritten by one commercial firm without others competing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) has touched on several matters, from reciprocity to the proper

method of floating a loan. I have always observed that when a matter is much upon one's mind, he frequently refers to it, and 1 am sorry to think that my hon. friend has not yet got over 1911. Time heals all things, but it does inot seem to have been effectual in the oaise of the defeat on the reciprocity issue. There is nothing further from my thoughts than political controveoBy. Since this war broke out, I, in common with other members of the Government, have had what I might describe as fairly heavy responsibilities, and I have not had any heart for political controversy of any kind. Therefore I shall not discuss with my hon. friend the reciprocity issue, which has been dead and buried, in my view, for some years now, except to call his attention to this: He speaks of borrowing from the United States. My 'hon. friend knows, as every hon. member in this House knows, that Canada has bought from the United States for years past much more than she has bought from any other country. Our imports from the United States have been enormous. When we make a loan we simply buy money. We are not doing anything different in buying money from the United States from what we have been doing for many years in buying goods from the United States.
