speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
To get back to
our muttons-my hon. friend has asked me a rather leading question as to the methods of financing our loans. I may say to him that in my view, in the public interest, it is not of advantage to discuss that phase of the question at present, but I do think it is fair, in answer to my hon. friend, to give him my views with respect to the matter of asking for tenders. It is perfectly clear to me, and it is the opinion of the best financiers, that for large loans, loans to governments, loans running up to $25,000,000, $50,000,000, $75,000,000, or $100,000,000, good results cannot be obtained by the tender system. It has never been followed in this country by any Government. The policy
adopted in the past is the policy which I have continued, and I believe it is the sound policy. We usually negotiate through the Bank of Montreal, and negotiation is carried on for a considerable period, and every precaution is observed to get a proper price for our securities, having regard to the market conditions. The loans are placed in the utmost good faith with the sole idea of doing the best possible for the Dominion. I think that has been proved with regard to all loans placed by this country; at least, I do not know anything to the contrary. The traditions of the Finance Department have been good, and I hope to hand them on unimpaired in that respect. Since this war broke out financial conditions have been most trying; they have been kaleidoscopic, as I have before stated. Transactions in time of war cannot be judged by transactions in the preceding period of peace. The minister finds himself in the position of simply doing the best he can.
My hon. friend has referred to the loan of $45,000,000 which we negotiated last August in New York. There was some criticism in the press, I think rather natural criticism, for this reason: Municipalities and provinces had been borrowing, or were about to borrow, and the community had not really become aware of the changed conditions which existed. I may say to my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) that in England, when the British Government departed from the 3i per cent standard, and got on the 4 per cent standard, and departed from the 4 per cent, and got on the 4i per cent standard, all the municipalities were more or less disturbed, because it established a new rate for loans. Let us take the situation that existed when I placed the $45,000,000 loan in August last. In my opinion, that was one of the most useful loans that had ever been placed by the Government of Canada. It served Canada admirably well, and it served the Imperial Government admirably well, and paved the way for the $500,000,000 Anglo-French loan. The loan which we negotiated last August aggregated $45,000,000: $25,000,000 one-year notes, maturing on August 1,	1917;	$20,000,000
two-year notes, maturing on August 1, 1918, coupled with a provision to take Dominion 20-year bonds at par, maturing in 1935.
I do not desire to go into details, except to say this: the rate of commission paid was exceptionally low, 'being three-quarters of one per cent. I do not know of any transaction that has been negotiated to bet-
No better man.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I heartily agree with my hon. friend in that. The loan was negotiated to a point where we felt it was an absolutely fair transaction, having regard to the conditions that there existed. We enlisted the support of the strongest interests in the city of New York. There are two things that must be borne in mind in connection with every loan. In the first place, regard must be had to the terms, and that is a matter of negotiation. The terms should be judged by the prevailing financial conditions. The second feature to which regard must be had is the fact that it is extremely desirable that a loan should be a success, that is to say. that the loan should reach a premium. I need not say to the members of this House that it is very desirable to have a market in which your loans are a success. There fore, that aspect of the matter must not be overlooked when considering the question of price. That loan was negotiated in New York, and it was one of the most useful loans ever placed by the Dominion Government. It was particularly useful having regard to the exchange situation prevailing last August, it was decidedly in the Im-

perial interest and it paved the way for the Anglo-French loan of $500,000,000.
To come back to the question asked by my hon. friend; it is a fact that a new basis was established for securities; that is to say, a new basis appeared to be established for securities, but in reality, as I stated to the general manager of the Bank of Montreal after the transaction had been concluded, the fact was that the basis had existed but it was not known that it did exist. The market had been an uncertain one. When bond houses would attempt to place securities, there was doubt as to what price should be paid, and .there was a certain difficulty in placing securities, but when the true price was established by the Dominion flotation in New York, the air was cleared and people knew what they had to face in the way of interest rates, and they faced them. The result has been that there has been a first-class market in New York for the higher grade of Canadian municipal and provincial securities.
This loan of ours in New York paved the way for the Anglo-French loan of $500,000,000. It is true that.there was some criticism in the presis in regard to my financing in New York. As I stated, that was natural, because the rate of interest was higher than we had ever paid before, but after all, the sound sense of the community soon realized that the war had entirely altered conditions and that the price was a fair one under the circumstances. Any doubts that any persons may have had at that time were dissipated when, headed by the Lord Chief Justice of England, a man who had had wide experience in finance, and representatives of the British treasury, the Imperial Commission, including a great banker of London, came over to negotiate the $500,000,000 loan. What was the result? The result was that the arrangements which had been made by the Canadian Government through the Finance Minister and (Sir Frederick Williams-'Taylor were more favourable than the arrangements made by the Imperial Commission. I had forgotten to mention that the gentlemen whom I have named were accompanied by representatives of the French Government. That Commission, representing, as they did, the Imperial Government and the French Government, and pledging their joint credit, were not able to obtain as good an interest rate, or to negotiate on as fair a basis of borrowing, as the $45,000,000 loan was negotiated on. Of course, no reflection whatever is made
upon the commission which negotiated the Anglo-French loan. I think they handled that very important matter with great tact and ability, buit the facts had to be faced, and among the facts are the interest rate and financial conditions.
It is very illuminating to read, in the financial history of the American Civil War, of the action taken at first by the Secretary of the Treasury in the matter of floating loans. They did not believe, of course, that the war would last so long as it did, and they were naturally reluctant to face market conditions or to face the high interest rates which prevailed. They had in mind that before the war they could borrow money for 3J or 4 per cent; they were reluctant to place themselves on a 6, 7 or 8 per cent basis, and some short date loans were negotiated, loans which fell due while they required to make further borrowings, and the result was that a very serious condition developed in their finances. The principle which I have been endeavouring to follow since this war broke out is this: I realized that there was a world financial condition which must be faced. You must face the facts. I have believed that this war is going to last a considerable time. I made up my mind that the true policy for the Government to pursue was to face the facts, to face the interest rate, and to avoid, so far as it was possible, short date borrowings. What I mean is this: In the first place, short date borrowings may provide for the time being, but you may need fresh borrowings for the purpose of the war; secondly, after the war there is always a period- of so-called reconstruction, in which it may be very necessary that you should have available your full credit resources for the purpose of the nation in that period. No matter who may be the Finance Minister of this country, no matter what the Government of the day may be, it is the duty of the Minister of Finance at this time to face the existing situation and borrow for longer dates rather than for shorter dates in order that these short date loans may not mature during the remaining period of the war, or in the period immediately succeeding the war. I believe that such a policy will meet with the approval of this House and of the financial and business community.
In regard to the $45,000,000 loan, I would very much rather have made a five or ten-year loan, but the conditions at that time were such that I could not make a five or ten-year loan, and the result is that I had to make a one or two-year loan, and I had

to give an option which at the time I would much rather not have given. The transaction was carried out to the best of the ability of those who negotiated it and in the result I think it stands put as rather a notable instance of a loan, negotiated for the first time in a foreign market, on exceptionally favourable conditions having regard to the market situation at that time.
I have dealt sufficiently with the matter of the Canadian loan of $45,000,000 in New York. Now, I come to another matter-mentioned by my hon. friend, and I think quite properly, and that is the question of economical administration. Since this war broke out, I do not know what policy the Government could have adopted that would have given better results along that line than we have achieved. As far back as a year ago last June-because this war was casting its shadow before us and financial conditions were very trying before the war broke out,-the policy was adopted of going ahead only with works under contract until conditions should improve. It is not the smaller expenditures that give us trouble, it is not the little wharf here or the little dredging yonder, or the customs house there, that add materially to the expenditures of the Dominion; it is the larger works which have been under construction. It might be asked: Why did you not stop last year the construction of the National Transcontinental railway? It would seem to be that public opinion would not support a Government in stopping that construction. It would only mean grave injury to the line and to all parts of it. We therefore could not shut down on the construction of the National Transcontinental ; nor could we very well shut down on the Quebec Bridge. It is true we could serve notice on the contractors, and break the contract. But the plant is there, and the contractors would undoubtedly have an action for damages. Then there is the further fact that the spans of the bridge that are already in place would undoubtedly deteriorate. We therefore decided to continue the construction of the bridge. The Welland Canal was also under construction. The Welland Canal project was embarked upon with the consent of both parties in this House before the war broke out. It is under contract for construction, the contractors have their plant there, and contract* for certain sections have been let; but no contracts for new sections have been let since the outbreak of the war. I have heard both my right hon. friend the leader [Sir Thomas White. 1
of the Opposition, and the hon.. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), in a discussion in this House before the war broke out, state that they were in favour of the enlargement of the Welland Canal, and also in favour of the Georgian Bay Canal. Therefore, I do not think that this Government can fairly be attacked for not having discontinued work upon these large enterprises, which take the major portion of our expenditures apart from the necessary expenditures on Civil Government. 1 assume that that is common ground. I do not know how this Government could have been more economical than it ha* been in regard to public works since the war broke out, for since about a year ago last June we have embarked upon no new works, except possibly some by way of repairs. We have discontinued new works, and gone on with works only eo far as it was necessary to go on with them, and if hon. gentlemen opposite can tell me how we could have been more economical than that I should like to hear their suggestions.
There is another point. At the time this war broke out there was a very trying period for general business for many months. There was a profound dislocation and interruption of business in this country, and I say it was a good thing for Canada that we had a fairly large programme of public works under construction at that time, because it minimized unemployment. It seems to me it would have been most unwise for this Government, at that, of all times, to have discontinued expenditures on public works, and further unsettle the entire community. My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), who I am sorry is not in his seat, referred the other night to increases in the public debt of Canada. I desire to say that no sound conclusion can be drawn from the mere fact of an increase in the public debt of Canada in any one year, or in any period of years. The real question is not whether the public debt has been increased, but whether the money borrowed has been wisely expended. I have never taken up this question of an increase in the public debt, except in defence of the Government when charges have been made, as they frequently have, that we had greatly increased the public debt. But, as the question has been raised, I desire, for the information of the House, and not in any controversial spirit, to lay upon the table the net debt of Canada from 1903 onwards. Speaking briefly, I may say that in 1903 the net debt was $261,000,000. In

1911 it was $340,000,000, or an increase of $79,000,000. I am not making any criticism as to that increase. In 1912 the net debt was $339,000,000. In 1913, the first year this Government was in power, the net debt was $314,000,000, or a reduction of $25,000,000. In 1914 the net debt was $335,000,000. In other words, on the- 31st day of March, 1914, (that is to say, at the end of the fiscal year before the war broke out) the net debt of Canada was less than when this Government took office by $5,000,000.	Then the war came on.
It is true that the net debt of Canada has increased for 1915 to $449,000,000. It is also a fact that, apart from the war, the national debt has increased by something over $50,000,000. But, the other night, when the hon. member for Pictou was dealing with this question, I referred to the fact that our revenues had been cut in half from August, 1914, the date of the outbreak of the war, onwards. Where we were getting $10,000,000 a month before, we got only $5,000,000 after the outbreak of the war. Maintaining our expenditures as I have already stated we did, for the purpose of minimizing unemployment in this country, and with our revenues decreasing until the tariff was brought down in February, only one result could accrue, and that was an increase in the national debt. But I do not believe that the fact of an increase in the national debt, by reason of conditions brought about by the war, is any just ground for criticism of this Government.
There is another point which, as the hon. member for Rouville has raised it, I may as well deal with now. Hon. gentlemen opposite, when Estimates have been up from time to time, have frequently repeated a statement which was made in the first instance by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley). That statement was made in the first instance by the hon. member for St. John on March 3, 1916, and appears in the unrevised Hansard as follows:
Mr. Pugsley: The hon. gentleman who is In charge of these Estimates (Mr. Hazen) will re, collect that the Minister of Finance stated that there were items in these Estimates aggregating about $29,000,000 which the Government thought it would not be called upon to expend in the coming year. If the minister would state the items in this department that go to form part of that $29,000,000, it would facilitate the work of the committee.
That statemient 'has 'been repeated by hon. gentlemen opposite time and again on the occasion of ministers taking up their Estimates. As a matter of fact, I
said nothing of the sort. What I stated in my Budget speech was that it was the policy of the Government not to proceed with works not actually under contract. What the hon. member for St. John adduced from that was this. He said: Your total Estimates are $188,000,000; you say you are going to have an expenditure of $160,000,000; subtract $160,000,000 from $188,000,000 and you have a balance of $28,000,000, which you say you are not going on with; will each minister therefore kindly explain the items that will be embraced in that $28,000,000? I need not say to this House that that is an absolutely fallacious inference. The hon. member for St. John proceded on the assumption that there was no difference between the Estimates and expenditure; that is to say, estimate of works that are being gone on with, and the expenditure that will be made upon them. It is well known that there are always lapses, and in order that the House may have full information on this point, and that there may be no repetition of a statement which is manifestly erroneously founded, without going back too far, I desire to call attention to the fact that in 19101911 the difference between the expenditure and total Estimates was $17,000,000; in 1911-12

the last year that my right hon. friend opposite was Prime Minister-the difference was nearly $30,000,000; in 1912-13 the difference	was	$35,000,000;	in	1913-14	thedifference	was	$41,000,000;	in	1914-15	thedifference	was	$46,000,000;	in	1915-16	thedifference	was	$32,000,000;	and in 1916-17
the difference is $28,000,000, that ie to say, the difference between the estimated expenditure and the Estimates actually laid upon the table of the House. Now the Estimates that have been laid on the table represent items which have been adopted by Parliament.
We have placed them in the Estimates because they have been voted before. The war has interrupted the progress-of these works, and I laid down the policy of the Government in the Budget speech when I stated that it would not be our policy to go on, during the period of the war, with those works not actually under contract. The reasons, of course, are obvious: Our expenditures for war are so great, and the financial demands upon us will be heavy. Apart from that, there is no necessity today for furnishing employment, because at the present- time it is very difficult to get help in this country for our industries.
Why did you keep those items in the Estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is, and always has been a difference between estimates and expenditures. I desire to read' a statement made by my predecessor, the Hon. Mr. Fielding, with reference to this very matter, because it is clear that the Opposition at that time had a habit, which seems to be followed by the Opposition of to-day, of raising the question of lapses. This question came up in 1907, and I have no doubt it has come up on almost every occasion on which a Budget speech has been delivered. Mr. Fielding, as reported in Hansard of 1907, volume IV, page 7859, said:
Mr. Fielding: I assume they are. I observe my hon. friend is not content with taking the ordinary appropriations of the year hut he takes everything that it is possible to take, everything that is in sight, everything that is not nailed. He takes the appropriations for the ordinary works, he takes the appropriations for capital account, he takes the appropriations for railway subsidies, he takes the appropriations for everything that can be thought of. Well, that is all legitimate enough as a statement of the appropriations of the year, hut it is apt to convey a very misleading impression ; it is apt to convey the impression that it is proposed to expend these moneys within the year. Now, as respects a considerable part of these moneys they are not expended within the year and are not [DOT] likely to be expended for several years. There are millions in that vote to which my hon. friend refers, which have been included in his calculation two or three times. Take the railway subsidies. We are voting not one dollar of new railway subsidies this session but a revote of appropriations of former years. They have appeared in the calculations of my hon. friend, they have appeared in his budget of gloom at the close of each session ; but they were not expended, they never added a dollar to the obligations of the Dominion of Canada. But now that they are being revoted they afford ar opportunity to my hon. friend to include them again in his budget. I am afraid some of them will turn up in future years and he will be able to include them again, because it is quite likPly that a number of these expenditures will not be made within an early time, though we would be pleased if they were. If we could be assured that every mile of these railways would be built within the next four years, far from complaining we would be pleased to have it so, because it would make for the general Improvement and development of the country.
Now, my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) happens to be here, and I made a reference to some remarks of his the other night. While I do not desire to repeat, what I said was in substance this.

I would like to ask my hon. friend if he regards the remarks of the Hon. Mr. Fielding as being at all applicable to the present situation. Mr. 
Fielding was speaking about a number oi appropriations for railway subsidies which certainly would not be paid until they were earned. If my hon. friend were asking for appropriations for railway subsidies, that would be a different matter; but we are not speaking about railway subsidies at the present time. Mr. Fielding was also speaking about public works in connection with which the amounts were not going to be spent in that particular year, but preliminary surveys were to be made, locations to be determined, etc. Does my hon. friend intend, under the items that he is including in these Estimates, to go on with the purchase of sites' for public buildings, to employ surveyors for the purpose of making surveys for public works, and to do preliminary work of that kind? That was what the Hon. Mr. Fielding was referring to, and he pointed out that it was impossible to use the money until the preliminary work was done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am sorry my hon. friend was not in when I was speaking before, because I discussed the matter pretty thoroughly. My hon. friend misunderstood the trend of my argument, which was this: The hon. member for St. John stated:
The hon. gentleman who is in charge of these estimates (Mr. Hazen) will recollect that the Minister of Finance stated that there were items in these estimates aggregating about $29,000,000 which the Government thought it would not be called upon to expend in the coming year. If the minister would state the items in this department that go to form part of that $29,000,000, it would facilitate the work of the committee.
This statement of the hon. member for St. John has been made on several ocea; sions in Committee of Supply. What 1 de-, sired to point out was that I made no such statement as that attributed to me. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Pugsley) reached his conclusions in this way: he said: Your Estimates are $188,000,000 and your expenditures for the coming year, apart from the war, will be $160,000,000 or a difference of .$28,000,000. Therefore there are in the Estimates items amounting to $28,000,000 which you are not going to expend. I pointed out, before my hon. friend came in, that that argument was erroneous for this reason, that with regard to those works, that are under contract at the present time, and which we are going on with, there will be lapses as there always have been, in the past, and I read a statement to the House in which I showed that in 1910-11 there

was a difference between Estimates anc( expenditures of $17,000,000; in 1911-12, of $29,000,000; in 1912-13, of $35,500,000; in 1913-14, of $41,300,000; in 1914-15 of $46,000,000, and, in 1915-16, of $32,000,000.

Does my hon. friend then mean to say that in regard to the Estimates this year in reference to which he said:
New works would not be undertaken until the financial outlook became clearerhe is not going to economize any more and not going to do anything different from what was d,one by the former Minister of Finance.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am sorry my hon. friend was not in the House, because I do not like to repeat all my argument, but I have so much respect for my hon. friend that I shall dwell on it a little.
5 p.m. When I stated the other night that I did not take the remarks of my hon. friend seriously, I said what I regarded was a delicate compliment to his intellect, because his remarks were, to say the least, strange. I stated what was the policy that we followed on account of the outbreak of the war and the enormous additional expenditure devolving upon the Dominion, and, I believe, it is a right policy. We determined, that we were not going on with new work until conditions permitted. I stated, in my Budget speech this year, that while the war was on our policy would be not to go on with new works which were not actually under contract.
Is that a new policy, or are you only doing what Mr. Fielding did?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Fielding gave me nearly all the troubles that I have had during the last four or five years. I was stating before my hon. friend came in, that it has not been the little armoury here, nor the little post office yonder, nor the custom house in the other place that has given us any financial difficulty.
You are not answering my question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am answering. The vast expenditure of this Dominion has been the expenditure that we have had to make in connection with the Transcontinental railway, the Quebec bridge, and other public works undertaken by the late Government.
The Welland canal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not want
to draw all the Liberal skeletons out of the closet and show them up here; I have had my troubles with them.
That is your own skeleton.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
When my hon.
friend from Pietou had the audacity, with a perfectly serene countenance and without a blush, to accuse this Government of being extravagant
I will do it again.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -when he knew that the great burden that is being placed on us has been in connection with work inaugurated by our predecessors and carried on by us, it is no wonder I said that I did not take my hon. friend seriously.

Would my hon. friend explain the marvellous increase in the expenditures in the Public Works, Post Office and Immigration Departments, and in the other departments to which I referred the other night? If my hon. friend is an economist, he is an economist of a new type. My hon, friend might also get away from generalities and tell me whether or not his including these items in the Estimates this year is inaugurating a new policy, or' whether it is only doing what Mr. Fielding spoke of doing in 1907.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it is a new policy in this respect: We have stated that until conditions permit we are not going on with certain items that appear in the Estimates. I never knew Mr. Fielding to announce that; I think his policy was to go ahead with all the works in the Estimates.

Does my hon. friend
think that the fact of leaving in the Estimates amounts which he says will not be spent does not affect the credit of Canada? Is it a matter of business to say: We ask this year $180,000,000, of which we intend to spend only $160,000,000? The money lenders obtain their information as to the outlay of the Dominion from the Estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I cannot imagine anything that would tend to strengthen the credit of the Dominion more than the statement that I have made. It is this: Parliament has voted many items in the Estimates the expenditure in connection with which we do not intend to go on with until conditions permit. It seems to me that



this is a strong position for the Government to take; that it makes not for the weakening, but for the strengthening of its credit. The trouble with the hon. member for Pictou is this: He is a man of fine intellectual quality, except when his intellect is clouded by partisanship. He has a temperamental partisanship, which on account of its intensity must be hereditary; I do not believe that he will ever get over it. If he were dealing judicially with a nonpolitical matter, I should accept his conclusions, but when he attacks this Government he throws fairness .and logic to the winds. My hon. friend says that we have increased the expenditure since 1911. Is there anything very wonderful in increasing the expenditure since 1011?
Yes, when you have no increase in the population.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Let us observe some of the tests by which national progress is evidenced. When this Government came into power the total trade of Canada was under $800,000,000. It grew to $900,000,000, to $1,000,000,000, and this year it is the largest in the history of Canada, $1,200,000,000. Look at the increase in the bank deposits, and judge the conditions in the country by that. My hon. friend referred to immigration. It is a fact that the immigration into this country in the years 1912 and 1913, until the outbreak of this war, was greater than it had been in the history of Canada. Hon. gentlemen opposite had engaged in great public works; they had engaged in the National Transcontinental railway. The corollary of their encouraging transcontinental railway building was that there devolved upon this Government a great deal of expenditure in connection with the development of ports-Halifax, St. John, Quebec, Montreal, Vancouver. We have had to make large expenditures for that purpose; we have had to meet enormous expenditures upon public works and undertakings inaugurated by the Government of my right hon. friend. The hon. member for Pictou says that our expenditures for 1914 were actually greater than they were in 1911. Well, that is not a very extraordinary matter. What about the expenditures of the Government of my right hon. friend in four-year periods? Could any one have the hardihood to say that the expenditure of the Government of my right hon. friend was no greater in 1911 than it was in 1907, no greater in 1907 than it was in 1903, no greater in 1903 than it was in 1901?
fSir Thomas White.]	'
That is the argument of the hon. member for Pictou. What are the facts? The total disbursement of the Government of Canada in 1900 was $52,000,000; in 1906, $83,000,000; in 1911, $122,000,000; in other words, an increase from 1906 of $40,000,000, or 50 per cent. I am not at this moment blaming my right hon. friend's Government for that increase, but it is a fact that that increase did take place. Yet the hon. member for Pictou says to us: you are blamable, you are chargeable, you are censurable, because your expenditure in 1914 was greater than it was in 1911. With all the expenditures which we had to meet upon the National Transcontinental railway and upon the other works that I have mentioned, and with the great development that took place in immigration and in all the business activities in this country, to me it would be a most marvellous thing if the expenditure had not increased. In any country the expenditures increase year by year. The hon. member for Pictou the other night challenged me to reply-he knew that he had the floor and that I had not-when he called attention to the growing debt. Well, would it not be a remarkable thing if, from1 1911 to 1915, under normal circumstances, there had been no increase in the national debt? What about the increase of the national debt during the period of the Government of my right hon. friend? My right hon. friend would not say that the debt of Canada did not increase during his regime, because the facts would rise up in contradiction. For four years previous to 1911, the national debt of this country increased by about $70,000,000. The largest reduction in the national debt is to the credit of this Government in the year 1912-13. I do not believe it is a fair basis of comparison to say: you increased the national debt so much, and we did not increase it as much. It seems to me that that is not a sound argument, and my hon. friend should not put it forward. The real question is not whether the national debt has been increased; it is, what has the national debt been increased for?

Is my hon. friend aware that his own leader characterized that increased expenditure under my leader as being so enormous and unjustifiable that it was evidence of corruption, and that he denounced that expenditure? If that logic was at all correct, and the Minister of Finance went on and increased the expenditure still further, what does he say that increase would be evidence of?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Did the Prime
Minister say it was evidence of corruption, or only prima facie evidence?
What is the difference?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should think
the increase in debt was so large for a few years, from 1907 to 1911, that the right hon. the Prime Minister of to-day (Sir Robert Borden) may have said it was prima facie evidence of corruption. Whether he said it was conclusive evidence of corruption, or not, I do not know; but certainly the fact remains that on the 31st day of March, 1914, the net debt of this Dominion was $5,000,000 less than when this Government took office, and for the four years before we came into office the increase in the net national debt of this country was about $70,000,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
How much
was it the following year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On the 31st day of March, 1914, the net national debt of this Dominion was $5,000,000 less than when we took office. I have explained to my right hon. friend what happened to the revenues of this country after the outbreak of war. I stated that our revenues had been cut in half, or were divided by three, after the outbreak of the war; that we deemed it a proper policy to maintain our expenditure on public works in order to minimize unemployment in the trying period following the outbreak of war; that it was the inevitable result of this that the national debt of Canada should be increased; and that it was a proper and a justifiable increase.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The reduction of the first year was only a prima facie reduction?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The reduction of the previous year was a real reduction, not a bookkeeping reduction, and we have to our credit the largest decrease in the national debt, namely, $25,000,000, that was ever obtained in any single year in the financial history of the Dominion. But I am the first to say that this argument of: We increased the debt to so much and you increased it to so much is illogical. You can draw no sound conclusion from it, and I never use these statistics except in rebutting attacks of an unreasonable character, such as. that made the other night by the hon. member for Pictou. ,
What about the expenditures?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think I have sufficiently dealt with that subject, and my hon. friend will have his turn on some other occasion.
I come now to a matter that has been drawn to our attention by the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean). I always listen to the hon. member for South York with a great deal of interest-in a way he is a prophet.

Thank God there are some.
Sir THOMAjS WHITE: But there are prophets whose vision is clear and true, and there are also prophets who, as to some-matters at least, are not necessarily true prophets-and then there are prophetesses like Cassandra, who was a true prophetess, although nobpdy believed she was a true prophetess. Whenever I listen to my hon. friend putting on his propaganda with regard to the currency I always think of the rainbow story. When I was a little boy I used to believe, in common with other boys, that there was a bag of gold at the end of the rainbow if we could only get to-the end of the rainbow, and' I used to look for that bag of gold, but I never found, it. The propaganda which my hon. friend preaches in his journal, and on the platform, and in this House, is very attractive. It opens up a golden vista, money, plenty of it, $100,000,000, $200,009,000, $500,000,000, $1,000,000,000-put your arms into it, plenty of money for all national purposes, the purposes of Canada, or the purposes of the Imperial Government. And what is it? National note circulation, reorganization of the currency, an issue of $1,000,000,000 of note circulation with $250,000,000 of gold against it. These are the panaceas of the hon. member for South York. I believe that my hon. friend from South York, for whom I have the greatest respect and admiration, is quite unsound in the financial views which he puts forth.
I feel bound to say that, because he has raised, at a critical time-at time when the people consider carefully every proposal put forward-what I regard as an impossible and impracticable and illusory financial proposal. My hon. friend says: Why not nationalize your currency; why not make the banks take Dominion note circulation and call in their notes? Well, if you did that, and it is possible to do it, it would mean that the banks would owe the Gov-

eminent in respect of the note circulation the amount of their present note circulation, and would put out Dominion notes to that amount. The fundamental mistake made by the hon. member for South York, if I may say so, is this: He does not realize that note currency, bank note currency or Dominion note currency, is only useful for circulation purposes; and that you cannot increase that circulation beyond a certain amount without in reality, making a forced loan without interest, either from the bank or from the community.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The banks have a certain note circulation whicji varies from time to time according to the commercial needs of the community. It is pocket money in the community, till money, so to speak. If a man gets a thousand dollars or two thousand dollars in bills, he does not carry them in' his pocket, but deposits them in the bank and, by the clearings the next day, the several banks that have issued the bills get back their notes and have to pay any balance against them in gold, or the equivalent of gold, viz., Dominion notes. My hon. friend says: Why not go to New York and borrow $500,000,000 or $250,000,000 in gold and then, to the extent of 25 per cent, make that gold a deposit against an issue of	$1,000,000,000, and then we
will have plenty of money for the meeds of Canada, plenty of money for ithe Imperial Government, plenty of money to purchase munitions and *carry on the waT. The idea is so apparently feasible, I might ask him: Why does not the Imperial Government gather up a thousand million dollars of gold and issue four thousand million dollars of paper money? Why does not any Government do that. It is very easy to turn on the printing press, even if you have a 25 per cent reserve of gold, but nevertheless, to the extent that the notes are not required for the circulation needs of the community, your paper has 'been watered; to that extent you have made a forced loan without interest; and the inevitable Tesult will be the depreciation of your currency. Let me give an extreme case. Supposing to-morrow the Dominion Government put out an issue of a thousand million dollars of paper. Who would take it? What would happen? The public would get it. They would take it in payment of services or for commodities, and they would deposit it in the *banks'. It would not be required for the 
circulation of the community, and the result would be that the banks of Canada would soon have tens of millions of dollars lying idle, not bearing any interest, and what would be the inevitable result? Why, a bank or a financial institution would say: We will take a bond because it bears interest, but we do not want a note, that is not needed for the circulation purposes of the country, lying idle and unremunerative in our'vaults. And what would be the result? Gold would go to a premium and your note would go to a discount, and the inevitable result of a large issue of paper money, an issue of paper money beyond the circulation requirements of a community, would be depreciation in your currency, destruction of your credit, and the loss of the gold that your country has. There is no doubt about that whatsoever. To-day the circulation needs of this country are met by the bank circulation and by the Dominion note circulation. Increase it by $10,000,000 and you get redundancy; increase it by $50,000,000 and yet get a great redundancy, and your notes are at a discount, and your gold at a premium. If there is anything we desire to avoid at this time; if there is anything calculated to damage the credit of the Dominion in New York or anywhere else, it would be to state that we were going to put out an issue of $1,000,000,000 of paper
I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
against $250,-
000,000 of gold. My hon. friend suggests the putting out of $1,000,000,000 worth of paper against $250,000,000 of gold on top of the present Dominion note circulation, for the purpose of financing our requirements and the requirements of the Imperial Government. I think the result would be depreciation. At the time of the American civil war, the North had to resort to paper currency, and so had the South. What happened? I may say that Germany is resorting to paper currency to-day.. The paper currency of the North went down to between 35 and 40, and it was fifteen years at least after the end of the civil war before the currency of the United States was restored to a parity with gold. What happened to the paper currency of the South? It became absolutely valueless: ten thousand would not buy a plug of tobacco. I stand, and intend to stand for sound finance, and I think that in this country, at this time, we should stand for sound finance, because it means so much to the credit of this country. A propaganda

of that kind at this time is, in my judgment a dangerous propaganda, because it holds out hopes to the people that cannot be realized. Speaking for myself, I do not know anything that would injure the credit of this country, that would prevent us from getting loans at a fair ihterest, that would impair our standing in the world more than an enormous issue of paper currency.
I come to another matter, my hon. friend's statement about federal reserve There is a great danger in attempting to compare the financial systems of different countries, unless you take all the circumstances into consideration. The United States system, before the establishment of the federal reserve banks, was a system of individual banks, not banks with branches, but individual banks; and on account of the requirements of the banking laws of the United States, the banks could only issue notes against national securities. These national securities were selling on an artificial basis, and the result was that it was not in the interest of the banks to issue sufficient currency to meet the needs of the country. That was the situation in the United States; it is not the situation in Canada. There is plenty of circulation here to meet the circulation needs of this country, but there was not enough circulation in the United States to meet the circulation needs of that country before the federal reserve system was created. For months after the war broke out, 1 kept in my office a comparative statement of the condition of the banks in Canada, of the British banks, and of the American banks, and I say that the degree of liquidity of the banks of this country was on all fours with the degree of liquidity of the best British banks. In other words, we adopt here the sound banking principles of Great Britain. Last fall, because I had read a good deal of the arguments advanced in favour of the establishment of a federal reserve system, I got a banker of this country to write to New York to ascertain officially whether the federal reserve banks in their discounting of paper of the banks of the United States were using any more currency than was required for the circulation needs of the United States. The answer was precisely what I had expected, namely, that the federal reserve policy is to issue only the amount required for circulation. In other words, the federal reserve banks of the United States occupy the same relationship to those individual banks in the United States, in the several regions, as the head
office of one of our great banks occupies to its branches.

Was that information
obtained from a federal reserve banker, or from the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I asked for the
information through the manager of one of the leading banks of Canada. I asked him to ascertain the facts from New York. There could be no other answer. If, as a matter of fact, the federal reserve banks were isuing more paper than the circulation needs of the United States required, the inevitable tendency would be for their notes to go to a discount. The thing is absolutely commonplace; it has happened frequently in the history of the world, and it will happen in the future.

I noticed, just before that law was brought into force, that at a meeting in New York of over 2,000 bankers of the United States, every one of the bankers condemned the innovation of federal banks. But I understand that these banks have worked out well since, so that the views of the regular bankers on that occasion would not seem to have been very sound; not that I am advocating the same system for Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think that the establishment of the federal reserve system in the United States was necessary, but, as I have pointed out, the situation there was fundamentally different from the situation in this country, because the United States had a system of individual banks. The head office of every large bank in Canada is, so to speak, a federal reserve bank qua its branches throughout Canada, because the head office takes money from one section of the country, where it is not needed, and transfers it to another section, and loans it out there. The result is that under our system, which is the same as the British system, the head office of the bank is the conduit pipe, so to speak, through which the money flows. Where it is not needed, it is transferred to a place where it is required. In adopting the federal reserve system, the United States adopted the precise principle of the British and Canadian banking system. Yhe idea was to make the currency more flexible, and to take the money from one section of the country where there might be an accumulation, and make it available in another place by way of loans to the banks in that other place where money was needed. That is the underlying principle of the federal reserve

system, but you cannot compare it fairly with the Canadian banking system. You cannot say: we will take a certain system from the United States and transplant it here. In England they have a bank of re-discount. It is very desirable, but it cannot be created overnight; it requires years to build up. The only way to build it up, apart from the ordinary mode of growth, would be to have the banks of Canada take shares in some central bank, just as the banks of the United States take shares in the federal reserve bank in the several districts. But, as I have pointed out, the head offices of the banks in Canada discharge the functions that the federal reserve banks discharge towards the individual banks in their several areas. I do not think that it is necessary, therefore, at this time to consider reorganizing the bank system of Canada. We have a war on our hands; there are extraordinarily trying days both at present and to be apprehended in the future, and it does seem to me that the banking system of Canada is, at the present time, working fairly well.
My hon. friend from South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) has referred to this credit of $75,000,000. He thinks the credit should not have been established, because it might impose too great a burden upon the Canadian banks. I desire to reassure my hon. friend. The banks of Canada have a very considerable accumulation of money upon their hands, and it is a matter of great pride that they are able to come forward at this time and offer such a large sum as $75,000,000 as credit to the Imperial Government. It is not a small sum; it is a large sum. Having disposed, whether satisfactorily or not, with the question of the issue of paper money, I desire to say this: From time' to time plans are put forward for creating credit, or for creating money. I do not know of any way of creating sound credit, or of providing money, exoept the old-fashioned way of saving it. What we have to learn in this country-this Government does not need to learn the lesson- is the virtue of saving and not putting our faith in panaceas and nostrums. We must put our faith in individual savings, in saving the money that men have obtained for their services, in saving the profits that men have made out of business. That is the only sound, safe, orthodox way of increasing the loan funds of this Dominion. As far as Governments are concerned, the Only way to finance them in time of war, is to reduce as much as you possibly can once your military expenditure commences

to grow, your ordinary expenditure, just as we are doing.
Oh, well!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Having gone that ' faT, how much farther could we go?
You might have reduced it by $25,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have gone so far as to reduce the expenditure and to make available all the resources of the country for the purpose of the war and for what is necessary in getting the money for the war. I am not going to use the term " credits." You often hear people say: We do not want any money, but give us a credit. What does that mean? It means money, it means just what you and I mean by the word term " money," and the only way of providing money for the war is by taxation or borrowing and paying interest rates, and not by forced loans from banks and the community.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: You are on dangerous ground there; think about your Insurance Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, the'insurance Bill is very fair legislation. The point I make is that you must keep up your revenues by taxation or you must keep it up by borrowing and paying the price. If you depart from that principle your policy will lead to evils which may be greater than war. I have spoken at greater length than I intended to on this matter, but in view of the argument of the hon. member for South York, the propaganda which he has put forward in his paper, and the expectations which might be raised by the suggested adoption of a policy which I believe to be unsound, although generally I agree with my hon. friend, I felt it my duty to deal with this question. I have stated the financial faith that is in me. Whether I have carried the judgment of the House or not remains to be seen.

I want to say a few words with regard to my hon. friend's reference to me in the course of his speech. My hon. friend ventured to question some remarks which I made in the course of the Budget debate but he has not explained the statement which I made that he was responsible for the debt of the country being increased to the extent of $51,000,000 over and above the cost of the Transcontinental railway and over and above those

other things of which he complains. My hon. friend has always been putting forward as an excuse for these alleged burdens that he had to provide for the National Transcontinental railway. We cleared all that question up in discussing the matter the other day, but it might be as well to remind my hon. friend, and I do not think he has forgotten it, that he was a believer in the National Transcontinental railway proposition in 1904. He did not then find any reason for withdrawing from the leadership of my right hon. friend in front of me (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) in 1904 or 1908. My hon. friend stood behind my leader and the Liberal policy of constructing the National Transcontinental railway right through until he took his position upon reciprocity. When my hon. friend comes and holds up his hands in holy horror about the Transcontinental railway, he should remember that it was a proposition to which he gave his full support previous to 1911. But I do not intend to follow my hon. friend in his desultory discussion of such facts as I have absolutely proven. But, there is another point that he has not explained to the committee and that is why he should persist in keeping in the Estimates sums aggregating $25,000,000 which he says he does not intend to spend.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are not in.

My hon. friend says: They are there and we are not going to spend them, but I am not going to take them out. Hon. members who are helped by their being in the Estimates have ventured to suggest that the war will come to an end perhaps, that the situation will be cleared and that between now and the 31st March, 1917, it may be possible to spend that money. The Minister of Finance knows that the commitments of this country - at this moment absolutely prohibit the possibility of his undertaking any new works or of availing hinmelf of any of these items which are included in the $25,000,000 if he is going to be a prudent Minister of Finance. My hon. friend reads for our edification a statement made by Mr. Fielding in 1907 in which Mr. Fielding went on to point out that the computation was made at the end of the year of the commitments and that it was improper to treat that the whole amount of money contained in the Estimates as being an absolute commitment because they might include a general vote for a project upon which preliminary expenditures, of necessity, had to be made,
that these preliminary expenditures took time and that, as a consequence, once a vote was initiated for any particular purpose in a given year of, say, $20,000, or $50,000, that did not mean that that $20,000 or $50,000 would be expended in that year because preliminary work had to be undertaken.
If that disproves anything at all in what way does it affect this?
Nobody wants to disprove anything.
You disprove your own argument.

I am presenting an argument founded on the quotation and I am dealing with the Minister of Finance on broad lines. The Minister of Finance puts that forward as a justification for having this amount in his Estimates this year. My hon. friend knows very well that what Mr. Fielding eaid in 1906 or 1907 with reference to the conditions prevailing at that time could have no possible reference to the conditions that exist in this year, 1916, when you are up against the most trying situation in all our history. Yet my hon. friend for some purpose-and there can be no purpose unless it is political-in the face of this financial situation, as my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) points out, persists in keeping before the eyes of the money-lenders, and of the parties to whom he has to go to obtain money, the idea that it is necessary for an expenditure of $25,000,000-

Mr	MACDONALD:-$28,000,000	more
than he says he intends to spend. Why does he keep it in the Estimates when he tells the money-lenders that he is not going to spend it. Can anybody find out why? If he is honest in regard to that statement -and I do not mean to impute any personal dishonesty to my hon. friend-what-can it mean? If that amount is there for no particular purpose then my hon. friend should say so. If my hon. friend does not intend to spend it why does he keep it there? He keeps it there in order that political pressure may be exerted under this or the other condition and in order that it may be possible to send a corps of engineers into a particular county to run up and down, plant stakes and do certain things that the electors who perhaps desire to have a public work may have held

before	them the alluring proepect
that it is to be gone on with. My hon. friend knows it. It is there for no other purpose in the world. My hon. friend knows very well that his attempt to justify himself by a statement of Mr. Fielding is simply begging the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend did not quite understand what I said. I stated that the hon. member for St. John had reached the conclusion that I had said there were 828,000,000 in the Estimates which it was not proposed to expend. By subtracting $160,000,000, the amount of the estimated, expenditure, from $188,000,000, the amount of the Estimates, we get a balance of $28,000,000. Now, the error made by the hon. member for St. John was in assuming that the $160,000,000 of estimated expenditure coincides with $160,000,000 of the Estimates. Now, the point I made, and in reference to which I quoted Mr. Fielding, was that the $160,000,000 of estimated expenditure represents much more than $160,000,000 of Estimates of works actually under construction. There are some items in the Estimates-how many I do not know -which are not under construction, and which will not 'be gone cm with for the present. But it is no such amount as $28,000,000. I think my hon. friend understands what I am driving at.
What the minister says is that the amount may not be $28,000,000, but that there are included in the Estimates certain works which will not be gone on with.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Until conditions permit.

My hon. friend
knows perfectly well that conditions cannot possibly permit of any new works being gone on with this year; I am speaking of the financial year, which begins on April 1. Will my hon. friend say that he can conceive of financial conditions under which he will be able to engage in new works this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
While I am prepared to make a general statement that we should not go on with works under contract until conditions permit, I would say to my hon. friend:	that from time ' to
time in the administration of this country it has become perfectly clear that it is in the^national interest that a particular work, even at a time like this, should be gone on with. For instance, some work in connec-

tion with ports or harbours may be absolutely needed. There were one or two cases like that last fall. I recall the case of Bathurst, N.B., -where some work had to be done in order that business might proceed. It would never do for me to say expressly and explicitly that this, that or the other item, amounting to so much, will not be gone on with under any circumstances. I am quite prepared to make a general statement, and I have already done so, but I cannot state explicitly that no single item will be gone on with, and my hon. friend knows it is unreasonable to ask me to do it.
I do not think my hon. friend would stand much cross-examination if we had him before a tribunal where we could cross-examine him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no desire to.

He really wants
to keep these items in the Estimates. Cases such as he has referred to could be covered by Governor General's warrants, and my hon. friend knows it. Can my hon. friend imagine any supervening public necessity that would justify the erection of a post office at some of the places provided for in the Estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is improbable but it is quite possible. Conditions in connection with rural mail delivery, for instance, might make it necessary. But I do not think it probable.	[DOT]

If a provincial
election were impending, would my hon. friend regard pressure from political friends as a supervening necessity? My hon, friend went out of his way to gratify his political friends in British Columbia, by imposing a duty on apples. Can my hon. friend conceive of his lending a soft ear to representations made by Mr. Bowser for certain public works in British Columbia, supposing he had to face the electorate in June? Does my hon. friend mean to say that he would turn a deaf ear to Mr. Bowser if he came along with any such proposals?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In all my experience as Finance Minister I have never, in the four years I have occupied that position, had any such request proposed to me, My hon. friend's experience during the preceding Administration has evidently been different. He is altogether too suspicious. I do not believe that any expenditure by this

Government in any constituency in British Columbia

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Could save the Bowser Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
or in any other
province, would have any effect upon a provincial election.

Other hon.
gentlemen might disagree with my hon. friend. If my hon. friend has not had communications from the Government of British Columbia, perhaps his genial friend the Minister of Public Works has whispered in his ear. Perhaps he is the medium through which the Finance Minister is approached on these questions. As I was saying, my hon. friend would not stand a very close cross-examination on the subject of the Estimates. We are bound, however, to take him at his word. He says that he has pledged his word to the people from whom he is going to borrow money that there is in these Estimates a large sum which will not be spent unless a superlative public necessity demands it. My hon. friend forgets what he said to the hon. member for South York a moment ago. Then he preached the doctrine of economy; savings, he said. Is my hon. friend going to moralize in regard to banking and finance and economy, and at the same time not put his theory into practice? My hon. friend will not declare that conditions in this country are such as to require the expenditure of this money in the Estimates which ought not to be there at all. If this money is not to be expended, it should not be in the Estimates. My hon. friend has not given any warrant why it should be there, and I say it is only for the purpose of leading people in different sections of the country to believe that certain works are to be gone on with in their part of the country. Where is the minister economizing? Take the Post Office Estimates, for instance, to which reference has already been made. In 1911 the expenditure was $7,954,000, and in 1915 $15,900,000. This year my hon. friend proposes an expenditure along that line practically the same as last year, if not greater. Is he economizing there? How is he economizing?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not want to interrupt my hon. friend unduly, but does he think that, on- a bare statement that there was a post office expenditure of $7,000,000 in a certain year, and that four years after there was a' greater expenditure, he has proved anything? My hon. friend
compares the post office expenditures of 1903, 1904, and 1905 with that of 1916, and asks: Are they larger or are they smaller? What about the rural mail delivery? What about the multiplied activities of the Customs Department due to our large increase in trade, 50 per cent over what it was in 1911? What about our parcel post system, which was established by the late Postmaster General? My hon. friend is too intelligent not to know that he has no basis of comparison when he puts an expenditure of $7,000,000, in 1907, against a larger amount in 1915, and says that that means extravagance. It does not mean anything of the kind.

When I add to my argument the fact that my hon. friend expends all this money and in addition has a deficit of $3,000,000 in the Post Office Department, I think that does mean extravagance. My hon. friend should cut his coat according to his cloth, and he should not spend in the Post Office Department more money than he receives from it. When, in addition to that, we remember that in regard to the Post Office Department it has been shown that there has been no economy at all, but a tremendous increase in the number of employees in the service throughout the country, my hon. friend should cease homilizing to the House about economy. As his leader said in regard to an expenditure, many millions less than what he is purposing to make this year, it is prima facie evidence' of corruption. If that argument in reference to the expenditure referred to was true, it is ten times as true with regard to the expenditure which my hon. friend purposes making, and I apply the words of the Prime Minister, who is the leader of my hon. friend, and say that this expenditure which he is proposing to the people of this country to-day is prima facia evidence of corruption.
At six o'clock the House resumed and then took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.
