maintopic: PETITION FOR DISALLOWANCE OF ONTARIO STATUTE.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PETITION FOR DISALLOWANCE OF ONTARIO STATUTE.
speechtext:
By your leave, Mr. Speaker, and
with the consent of the House, I should like to say a word in answer to a question that was put this afternoon when the Prime Minister and myself were not present. The question was asked, I believe, by the hon.

member for Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) as to whether a petition had been received asking for the disallowance of recent legislation in the province of Ontario providing for the appointment of a school commission. The Minister of Public Works, who was leading the House <sA the time, answered that he had not personal knowledge of the petition. I desire to say that the hon. Minister of Public Works was not present when the petition came before Council. Such a petition was received; it came before Council, and it has been referred to the Lieutenant Governor of Ontario for any observations that he may desire to make upon it. That is the course which is followed whenever a petition is made for disallowance of an Act of the legislature of a province.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: Consideration resumed in committee of the proposed resolution of Sir Thomas White to authorize the Governor in Council to raise by way of loan an additional amount not to exceed the sum of $75,000,000; Mr. Rhodes in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before the committee proceeds I feel it my duty to remind hon. gentlemen of the rule which governs the discussion of subjects such as we have before us. It is found in subsection 5 of section 13, and reads:
Speeches in Committee of the Whole must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
The discussion this afternoon took a very wide range; so wide, in fact, that the greater portion of it was not, in my judgment, relative to the item under discussion. Various reasons contributed to the wide range of the discussion; I do not know that any useful purpose can be served by referring to them in detail. I trust, however, now that I have brought the rule to the attention of the committee, that greater care will be exercised during the remainder of the sitting to see that the discussion, if not brought within the strict letter of the rule, may be at least brought within the spirit of it.

So far as my remarks this afternoon were concerned, I think they were germane to the question before the committee. I desire now for a few moments to reply to some of the observations that were made upon some of my remarks during the course of the discussion.
I am as anxious as you are, Mr. Chairman,

to observe the rules and to further the adoption of the resolution now before the committee, but I think that I am entitled to reply to some of the arguments that came up this afternoon, and to the criticism of the Minister of Finance of some of the views that I expressed. I have the greatest respect for the minister. I have watched his career in this House; it has been a rapid rise; in the eyes of the people of Canada it has been the satisfactory development of a public man. But if there is one thing a Minister of Finance ought to avoid it is the temptation to think that he knows it all; the temptation, I will not say to be egotistical, but to assume the attitude that he is in possession of the gospel of the finances of the country. Above all, he ought n<?t to patronize or to belittle the argument of an opponent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Of a supporter, you mean.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What is a
modern system of banking?

A modern system of banking is to nationalize the banking and not to make it a private monopoly. I understood the Minister of Finance this afternoon to say that a monopoly of the currency issue of this country should be in the banks. I say that the monopoly of the currency of this country ought to be in the nation, and it ought to be issued by the nation, and the whole credit of the nation should be used for the necessities of the country, both for the war and for other public needs. So I am not preaching an heretical doctrine, nor am I a false prophet.
The hon. gentleman suggested that perhaps I was likeCassandra, that I spoke something to the Trojans that they did not believe, but that yet proved to be true. The difference between the Trojans and the people at this time is that the Trojans did not know that what Cassandra had prophesied was true, while we do know, and the Minister of Finance knows, that the modern system of banking that obtains in Europe has been tried, is sound, and is in the public interest. And yet if anybody in this country suggests a more modern system of banking for Canada than we have had in the past, he is branded as a false prophet. I take issue with this argument, and I say that we can ourselves as a nation and by reforming our system of banking raise the money we want for the requirements of this war. The Minister of Finance says we should not bring on such a question now, in time of war. But that was the very time that Lloyd George and the British Government put it into practice.
Therefore I say that the Minister of Finance should have exercised a little more care in criticising the method I suggested, because he is practising in some degree every suggestion I made. He is using the national currency of Canada to help hiin out of the difficulties he has experienced; he is practising a system of re-discounts, and re-discounting for the banks. He issued a proclaimation to the banks of

this country and to others; he has even re-di&counted propositions that did not come to him through the banks, although I take it that the law in the beginning was limited in that way. So he relies on a national currency in an emergency and he is relying on a system of national re-discount in order to aid the banks. Do you not see the great and practical result of this system of re-discounting? We think it is a discredit to a bank to re-discount; with us a bank that re-discounts is supposed to be in difficulty. The Bank of England re-discounts whenever it wants money, and so do all big banks, because every bank knows that if it can re-discount it has not to conserve and keep itself strong in reserves and . liquid securities. As a consequence our banks cannot do as much for their customers at critical periods, because they say: "We -must keep enough to take care of the securities we have out, and of our depositors, should they call for their money.''' Butt when a bank knows that in a financial stringency, and in a situation like what we have to-day, they can re-discount the paper they are carrying in a national bank, they have much more money for the use of their customers, for carrying on the trade of the country, and for giving the people money sufficient to carry on their business. That is my argument, and it is not a new argument. It is not a.' new doctrine; it is not a heretical doctrine. If there is heresy in it, then the Minister of Finance is practising it every day. He has never come forward and said he proposed to stop re-discounting in this country, or that he proposed not to avail himself of the national currency. He uses both. He also committed himself the other day to a promise that he would take up and bring forward in this House a system of credit for the benefit of the farmers. They have that in every other country except the United States, and they are going to take it up there. They have it in France, in Ireland, in Germany, in Italy, and in Russia.
To nationalize the banking system of Canada, and the currency of Canada, as I proposed here this afternoon, is, I maintain, directly along the line of the proposition before this House. I am not to be placed before the country as proposing paper money, Us wanting to keep a printing press going. More and more, the world is being financed on credit, and the representation of credit is a document of some kind which comes from the printing press. But the credit is there behind it. Gold is becoming less and less a factor in the credit of a nation, of the 
individual and of a bank. Banks do not deal in gold; they deal in credit, and the more credit they have and can give to their customers, the better it will be for the business of the country.
Just one other thing, when I am talking of nationalization. Mr. Lloyd George not only nationalized the currency and put the State behind the banks, but he nationalized the railway system of Great Britain. The big thing for a nation in the day of trial is to nationalize things, to mobilize its securities for the benefit of the nation, and to mobilize its resources. If that is heresy it is only heresy in Canada I hope it is not heresy in this House. I hope that it is not a matter for ridicule that a member of this House should propose such modern, and, I think, such sound ideas of finance.
I am going to close with two very short statements. If we cannot have nationalization of our currency and of our banking, and the mobilization of our resources for the benefit of the country, we will be a second rate nation on this continent, for they have more of that in the United States than we have. So far as I am concerned, the day cannot come too soon which puts Canada on an equality with the United States and gives us as good a banking system as they have there. They have improved their system; it is much better than ours, and the proof of it is that there is abundance of money in the United States, the rate of interest is lower, and they are becoming the bankers, not of the world, perhaps, but of this continent. I take issue with any one who says that the banking and currency of the country should not be put on a national basis. If we cannot have it in this House it may be that the time has come to have a national party in this country that will bring about these things. We have a rather serious condition of affairs in this country, which may require to deal with it a national government and a national party, irrespective of old methods and practice. But whether that be so or not, I know that the people of this country, I know that the farmers of this country, whether in the East or in the West, believe in using the credit of the nation, the power of the nation, its resources, and its strength for the solution of the problems that present themselves to-day. The banks of Canada cannot save the Canadian situation; the nation must save itself, and it must do so on the lines I have suggested. The banks were not able to save the situation in England, and they have not been able to do it in the United

States, or anywhere else. But the countries using the national credit and the national currency, well secured by gold, have done so. It is all very well for the minister to represent me as saying here this afternoon that I propose to put the printing press to work and to send out a billion dollars' worth of securities. I did not use an illustration along that line, because I think we ought to have a gold reserve in this country to the amount of $250,000,000. When I spoke of issuing a billion dollars, I had regard for the present Dominion notes and the bank currency which, together; amount to more than $250,000,000, probably nearly $300,000,000. I do not want to misrepresent the minister, but I gather that he thought I was suggesting an inflated paper currency to be issued to such an extent that it would clog up the banks. I made no such proposal, but I ask him if he thinks that is likely to happen. Has it happened in England since they have adopted the system of re-discounting the state issue of notes? Has it happened in the United States? Are the banks clogged up there? I do not think so. They have a better system than we have. We have not got a national currency, nor a national system of banking, nor re-discounting, though perhaps we have made approaches to it. We have improved the situation, and I am urging the minister to go on in the practice he has already introduced, and not to belittle the practice which he has observed. When he talks about a proposal to issue notes of an unlimited amount, which would clog up the banks and reduce the credit of the country, I cannot see the appropriateness of his argument. Now that he has begun the system to which I have referred, I hope he will continue, and that he will come forward yet, not with a proposal to borrow $75,000,000, as in this case, with the Prime Minister coming along with a war .. proposal of $200,000,000, but to come forward, as the British Government did under the leadership of Lloyd George, with a large system, using the national credit, the national currency, and national banking. Then we would be able to clean the situation up in a much better way than is possible under the proposal now before the House or under the other proposals that are to follow.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I certainly do not desire to speak in any way as one having authority, but I am, at this time particularly, very jealous as to the credit of this Dominion; and I say that I do not know anything more likely to injure, or to derogate from, that credit than a suggestion to increase our issues of paper money.

Properly secured by gold. I disagree with the minister there.
'Sir THOMAS WHITE: My hon. friend refers to the situation in Great Britain, and to the situation in the United States. I therefore think that my hon. friend has not been at the pains to understand the situation that exists in Great Britain and in the United States. Before this war broke out, my hon. friend knows, the currency of Great Britain, that is to say the circulation medium of Great Britain, consisted of Bank of England notes, which were issued only against gold, and gold and silver in the hands of the nation. The essential difference between the situation in the United Kingdom and in Canada was this, that in England so much circulation was coin, while in Canada, on the other hand, circulation was principally paper money-paper money issued by banks secured by their entire assets, and Dominion note circulation secured by gold. If my hon. friend would take the trouble to look up the facts he would learn that Great Britain has not inflated the currency beyond the circulation needs. Great Britain was desirous that gold should not be hoarded and should not be exported, and, to meet the situation which arose at the outbreak of war, the proper expedient was adopted, availed of only to a slight extent-
To the extent ol hundreds of millions of pounds.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Millions is only a relative term, but the point I am making is that the note issue of Great Britain has not been increased beyond the circulation needs of the community. If it had to be so increased, only one result would follow -it does not make any difference whether it is Great Britain or any other country. If circulation becomes redundant then currency goes to a discount, gold goes to a premium and the exchanges of the world begin at once to run against that country. In time of war, if the stress is severe enough, nations are driven to expedients, and it has occurred many times in the history of the past that in order to meet the financial situation created by war-Germany is doing this to-day,

note issues are inflated. But there is only one possible result from note inflation, and that is rise in prices, depreciation of the currency, gold at a premium, and the exchanges of the

world beginning to run against the country which has inflated its currency. This was done in Germany. Germany has oyer-inflated its currency, and the result is the depreciation of the German mark on the exchanges of the world. Therefore, Great Britain's note issue did not mean that at any time Great Britain had issued notes beyond the circulation needs of the country. What has happened is that notes have gone out and gold has come in. Gold has been conserved. Notes have largely taken the place of gold as a circulation medium.
That is what I propose we should do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As in this country, the fact remains that the circulation needs of Great Britain are well beyond the note issue of Great Britain. My hon. friend also speaks about the United States. He states that the banks of the United States, they having nationalized the currency, as he says, are able to extend credit for the movement of crops. The way that the Government of the United States assists in moying the crops is by adapting perfectly legitimate financial means. What are those means? They make deposits, just as the Dominion Government might to-morrow make a deposit in a bank, with the banks of the United States engaged in business connected with the movement of cotton and grain. That is perfectly legitimate finance. The treasury of the United States has a fund on hand.
It issues national notes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
But these national notes have gold against them. The treasury makes deposits by cheque with banks in the usual way, an<} these banks, just like any other bank, having large cheques on deposit from the Government, have further facilities, perfectly legitimate, for carrying on this added business during the crop-moving period. But that is a very different thing from the Government of the United States handing out to banks unsecured paper money, or secured only to the extent of 25 per cent. I do not mean to say that there is not some leeway as to the amount of circulation that shall be secured, but that is a question of degree. In this country, for many years, the leeway has been 522,500,000 in connection with Dominion notes; that is to say, that everything beyond that was secured in gold. But circulation to the extent of $22,500,000

was what was called free circulation. Why? Because, as a matter of fact, the Government could always count upon $22,500,000 being out in circulation among the people in one and two dollar bills. But the fact remains that if we in this country were to adopt any such expedient as I certainly gathered my hon. friend had in mind, namely, to issue a large amount of paper money for the purpose of providing credit here for the purchase of munitions, even if secured by 25 per cent of gold, one result must follow, and that is that the currency would become depreciated, gold would go to a premium and the exchanges of the world would begin to run against this country. I am perfectly certain that if $50,000,000 of additional paper money were put into circulation in this country there would be a marked redundancy in our currency. I have no desire to discuss this matter on anything but a fair basis. I submit these considerations to my hon. friend from South York because I am satisfied that he is wrong and that he has not investigated these matters in the other countries to which he refers sufficiently to enable him to understand them. There is a great deal of difference between a Government making deposits in a bank, of funds collected in the usual course of the Government's business, and a Government handing out paper money to a bank if the bank must take that paper money beyond the circulation needs of the country. We did in this country what they did in Great Britain, only we did it very much more quietly. After a war has broken out in Europe, the first action on the part of a Government, in * order to conserve ite gold, is to suspend the Bank Act. That only means that instead of paying out in gold they are ready to pay out a circulating medium. In this case the situation was met in England by the issue to a reasonable amount, having regard to the circulation needs of the country, of the notes of the treasury. The very fact that this announcement is made at once stops panic and gold is not taken out of the bank to any considerable extent. Action of this kind is only intended to avoid the consequences of panic. I have no possible objection to my hon. friend putting forward his views as to what he believes to be a needed reform in our banking system; nor do I say it is impossible to nationalize the banks of Canada if it is not thought desirable to do so. But my hon. friend has stated that instead of al-

lowing the banks to issue notes, he would have the Dominion Government issue notes through the banks allowing them, I gathered from what he said, one per cent upon the amount so issued. We have to deal with the existing situation. The existing situation is that the banks had notes out in circulation to the amount, last year, of $100,000,000. If it were desired to nationalize the banking system, issue Dominion notes to that amount and require the banks to get in their bank notes, the situation would be that the banks would owe the Dominion Government $100,000,000, representing the amount of the notes which the Dominion Government had deposited with them and they would have to issue those to bring in their note circulation. It is true that the Dominion Government would be owed this large sum of money, but the question arises as to what the effect of that would be.
Now, this is a large question, and as the chairman has observed, it is irrelevant; but it is an important question, and I do not like to leave the discussion in this House and before the country without expressing my views upon it. I stated this afternoon that as Finance Minister I consider it my duty to express the *faith that is in me. My hon. friend has talked about world credits. The difficulty is we are apt to become confused in our terms. We hear about mobilizing resources, re-organization of our finances, of commerce and industry, and about establishing rural credits, and it is necessary to ascertain precisely what we mean by these terms. A rural credit does not mean anything more than this: that by legitimate financial methods a certain sum of money is placed at the disposal of the farming community to be availed of by way of loans. The fact that you call it a credit does not in the least alter the fact that what you are dealing with is money in the ordinary acceptation of the term. It would be possible for this Government, as for the United States Government, to establish a rural credit system, but that rural credit system, if sound, would have to be based upon existing sound methods of finance. That is, if rural credit societies or land banks were established, the United States Government could make deposits with those banks, or finance them by other perfectly legitimate methods, for the purpose of extending credits throughout the United States. I do not mean to say they have that in view, but that would be a feasible course, and would not be unsound financing, because
the money would be advanced in the ordinary way. My hon. friend seems to have the view that the money would be advanced, not in the ordinary way, but by handing over United States notes to these societies and banks.
I did not say anything of the kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend did not say that, then his argument, as I understand it, is only this: the Government of the United (States, or the Government of any other country could establish these credits by the ordinary sound financial methods of to-day. That is a very different thing from issuing paper currency. If I misunderstood my hon. friend, and he says that I did, I am quite ready to make amends, but I certainly did not desire to misrepresent him on this important question. But I say that to finance the Dominion Government in this stress of war, and to finance Imperial purchases here to the extent that my hon. friend has in mind- because he spoke rather slightingly this afternoon of a credit of $75,000,000-by an issue of Dominion notes secured by 25 per cent of gold, could only have the consequences which I mentioned this afternoon: there would be a redundancy in the currency, there would have to be a forced loan without interest, the notes we depreciate, exchanges would run against this country, prices would rise, and it would lead to many evils that are well known, to students of economic history.
It did not happen in the United,States.

I will only keep the committee a few minutes, and I hope I shall keep well in mind the suggestion which you, Mr. Chairman, with great pertinence have given to this committe. If I may be permitted I should like to say that in doing so you have given one more proof, if it were needed, that at the present time, both as to the speakership and the chairmanship of committees, we are particularly well-officered. I think the committee is indebted to my hon. friend from South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) for having drawn from the minister a very lucid explanation of what I have always understood to be sound views on currency. I hope my hon. friend from South York will not be offended if I say the minister has at the same time demonstrated that when a minister has a difference with a

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hope so.

While the- balance of trade is being aggravated against us from the United States, I have another remark and another suggestion to make. It is a curious fact, if my memory serves me aright, that in the last fiscal year, when we bought $123,000,000 worth more from the United States than we sold to them, we sold to the United Kingdom $121,000,000 worth more than we bought from them. In the language of baseball, we allowed the United States to put one over us in order that we might put one over Great Britain. Well, that is a very horrible state of affairs to have been brought about by an imperialistic and patriotic party such as I see opposite to me, to allow the United States to perpetrate this thing against us so that we might perpetrate a similar horror against the United Kingdom. It ought to give every man on the right side of the House the shivers-but such is the fact. I will repeat the figures for the sake of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works, because I am not sure that he is very good at figures. We bought from -the United States $123,000,000 worth more than we sold to them, and during the same year we sold to the United Kingdom $121,000,000 more than we bought from them. It appears to me a strange course to be followed by a wise Minister of Finance of an imperialistic party, a party which came into power pledged to increase the business of this country with the United Kingdom, and if possible almost to destroy it with the United States. I know the minister did not know about that placard, but the placard was hung over the streets of Ottawa all the same-no truck or trade with the Yankees. This party came into power pledged to increase our trade with the United Kingdom, within the Empire, and to decrease it or at any rate to frown upon it with the United States. They have increased it with the United States, and they have diminished it within the Empire.
Now, what should they have done? A

wise minister-I was going to say an allwise minister, but my hon. friend does not know it all or I would not have to tell him inow what I am telling him; he does not practice what he knows anyway, and this would be a much better world if we all did as well as we know, and my hon. friend the Minister of Finance is one of the greatest sinners in that respect, because he knowTs a great deal more than he practices, and I want to bring his practice up to what he knows-he knows that at the very time he should have given free wheat in order to increase our exports to the United States, so as to change the adverse balance into a favourable one, he should not have put an extra 5 per cent duty against goods coming from Great Britain, but rather he should have reduced the tariff against that country, or have rubbed it out altogether, so as to get more from them. Then we would have been taking some steps to have prevented the United States from putting one over us, and we should have ceased, especially at this time when the balances are so difficult for the British Chancellor of the Exchequer, to embarrass the Old Country to the extent they are doing by exporting so much more to her than we are importing from her.
I am sure the Minister of Finance will admit that I have not taken up much of the time of the House and I have not spoken in a controversial spirit. I am prepared with him to let by-gones be by-gones about words. If he will never mention reciprocity again, neither will I. But he must meet me half way; while he gives up the word, he must help me to establish the trade; that is the great thing. It is no joking matter, Mr. Chairman, because this money that we are borrowing will have to be paid back. Individuals may escape debts, but a respectable nation like Canada cannot. We shall have to pay this debt back, and we shall have to pay the interest on it. The minister has tremendous problems before him in the immediate future; I do not want to aggravate them by wasting his time. I hope that the minister will not make a long speech in reply to the remarks that I have made. I want him to think very seriously, almost prayerfully, about what I have said, before he makes answer at all, because when his answer comes I want it to be the right kind of answer. I want to bring home to him what is already very close to him, the terrible problems that he has to face in the future of this country in the way of paying these debts and of putting our trade upon

a proper basis. Let him become a free trader as he used to be in his youth. They say that a man is very rarely wholly untrue to his early beliefs, and I have great faith in the elasticity and breadth of mind of the Minister of Finance. If ever a national party is formed in this country, with all my respect for the member for South York I do not think he will be the man for that party; I think the Finance Minister will be the man. And, if he will get back to the ideas of his youth and not go on doing this horrible, excessive trade with the United States and do more trade with Great Britain, I shall be one of the most humble of his followers. I hope that he will take into consideration, anyhew, the horrible state of the balance of our trade that has come about since he came into power. I hope that he will consider the matter and adopt as much as he can of my suggestion.

The remarks of the hon.
member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) have been very interesting; equally interesting has been the answer of the minister. The hon. member for South York says that the banking system of the United States has been brought to a state of perfection. It is a fact that during the last three years the United States has spent over $50,000 in making investigation of the subject of rural credits. After careful investigation, it has been found that the ordinary banking system of that country fails to meet the needs of the farming community. Last year several Bills were introduced into the United States Congress, but none of them were sufficiently comprehensive to be finally adopted. The matter was left with a joint committee of Congress and the Senate last year to devise and present a Bill for adoption at this year's session of Congress. With all its good features, it would seem that the banking system of the United States does not meet the varied needs of the agriculturalists and of the industrial communities. The minister is to be congratulated on broadening the lines of banking so as to provide a better system of credits for our farmers. I am sure that before thus responding to a popular demand and an urgent need, he must have given the matter a good .deal of consideration. As the needs develop, the minister will broaden and extend the banking system in such manner as to provide adequately for all the needs of Canadian agriculturalists. The steps which have been taken will prove a great stimulus to agriculture and its allied in-

1S43
dustries. Just in proportion as the desirability of intensive farming is urged upon our farmers, so much the greater will be their need for banking accommodation. The minister, therefore, has made a progressive step in this respect, and it gives me pleasure to congratulate him for doing so.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
