speechtext:
The House in Committee of Ways and Means, Mr. Rhodes in the Chair.
On paragraph 1-interpretation clause:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There is a change in this from the resolution as first introduced. The first resolution read:
1. That, in the following resolution, " Minister," means the Minister of Finance of Canada; " non-Canadian company " means an incorporated company having its head office or principal place of business outside of Canada, but having assets in or carrying on business in Canada-
The minister has added:
-either directly or in the name of another company.
Is any machinery provided for ascertaining if a foreign company is carrying on business in Canada in the name of another company, either directly or indirectly?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The only machinery will be the machinery of the department in administering the Act. The Act will have to be administered by officials, and it will be the duty of the officials to inform themselves in such manner as they may be able as to the facts in such a case. The object, of course, is to prevent evasion of the terms of the Act through a foreign company, which is not doing business
116 J
directly in Canada, being permitted to carry on business through another company.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Are there any such companies doing business here in the name of other companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not to my knowledge at present; but I think it is necessary that the Act should cover the case.
Does the Copper Company come under this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not this particular section.
The definition of the word "person" is so broad that it would seem to cover an incorporated company, either a limited liability company or any other incorporation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The word was so defined in order that it might be used throughout the Act to represent not only individuals, but firms, partnerships, associations, incorporated companies or other corporate bodies.
On paragraph 2:
There shall be levied and paid to His Majesty a tax of twenty-five per centum of the amount by which the profits, earned in any business exceeded, in the case of a business owned by an incorporated company, the rate ef seven per centum per annum, and, in the case of a business owned by any other person, the rate of ten per centum per annum upon the capital employed in such business. Such tax shall be levied against and paid by the person owning such business for each and every accounting period ending after the thirty-first day of December, one thousand nine hundred and fourteen.
Provided, however-
(a)	'that the amount paid or payable by any person under the provisions of part one of the Special War Revenue Act, 1915, shall be deducted from the amount which such person would otherwise be liable to pay, and the minister shallhave power to determine any questions that may arise in consequence of any difference in the several periods for which the taxes under the said Act and those proposed herein are payable ;
(b)	that the dividends received from the stock of any incorporated company which has paid a tax upon its profits under the provisions of any Act based upon these resolutions shall not be included when the profits of any business are being determined ; and
(c)	that the amount of any tax paid by a person under the provisions of the Finance Act (No. 2) 1915, passed by the Parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland or under any legislation for raising revenue for the present war in force in France, Russia, Italy, Belgium, Servia, Montenegro, Japan or the colonies or dependencies of any of

these countries in respect of the profits of any business liable to taxation hereunder shall be deducted from the amount of the tax that would otherwise be payable by such person.

Did this point ever strike the minister, that the war loan being exempt from this taxation, if the whole $100,000,000 of the war loan were subject to the taxation of 25 per cent, the rate of that war loan would be pretty high. For instance, per cent is, in round figures, the rate payable on the war loan. Thus there would be about $5,000,000 annual income in interest payments to the holders of these bonds. If the minister will figure that out he will find that in the three years, if this whole amount be exempt, the Government will lose by this exemption in "'taxation something over $3,000,000.
Looking at it from the other angle, those who are exempt will receive a rate, on account of that exemption and including the 51 per cent interest of about 6:1 per cent on their money. In other words, taking the exemption, and the rate of interest paid by the Government on the war loan together, the war loan is costing the country about 6| per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not follow my hon. friend. I think he is assuming that the war loan is held by the businesses that will be subject to this tax.
That is my presumption.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows that the war loan is held by some
25,000	individuals, firms, and companies throughout Canada, and it is probable that a considerable amount is held by businesses which become subject to this taxation proposal. But my hon. friend has no doubt observed from the text of the resolutions that we do not impose any tax until the rate earned is 7 per cent in the case of companies, and 10 per cent in the case of individuals. Therefore, it would not immediately apply to the revenue derived from the loan. A company which held a part of the war loan, and whose net profits were estimated, would be entitled to say, so far as the interest upon the war loan is concerned, that it was exempt from taxation, and that it should not be taken into consideration in imposing this tax.

Take a concrete example. The banks hold $25,000,000 of that loan. They pay more than 7 per cent, consequently their excess profits would be

taxed. The $312,500 which they will save in one year, will, in three years, amount to something like $1,000,000. Perhaps Ihave not made myself clear. Exemption from this tax will save the banks, on the $25,000,000 of the loan which they hold, $312,500, and in three years, the period for which the loan runs, they will benefit to the extent of over $1,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think my hon. friend ia confused, if he will pardon me saying so. The banks hold a certain amount of the war loan. They did hold, I think, about $20,000,000. I doubt if they hold $20,000,000 now, because there has been a good demand for the loan, and it has been gradually absorbed. Let us assume, however, that they hold $20,000,000 of the loan. In estimating the amount that any bank would pay under this proposal, we should have to consider the net profits of the bank, and in estimating the net profits, regard would be had to the gross profits, and to the cost of administration. Among the gross profits undoubtedly would be the interest upon these securities. But, as I pointed out, the interest is less than 7 percent on the amount invested in them. I do not think that the banks would save in respect of holding these securities, except that it might be said that, if instead of holding these bonds they held some other securities that yielded over 7 per cent, they would be liable to pay a little more. But, after all, if my hon. friend considers the total assets of the banks of Canada, from which they earn their gross profits, the sum of $20,000,000 is relatively a very small amount. My hon. friend knows that it is necessary in floating a loan, in time of war especially, to provide that it shall be exempt from taxation by the Dominion. If vve had an income tax in this country, I have no doubt that private individuals would buy the war loan, as they have bought securities in the United States and other countries that are exempt from taxation for the purpose of avoiding the claims of the income tax. But I think it has no real bearing upon the principle of the Bill, if my hon. friend will permit me to say so; nor is it objectionable, so- far as I can see, that the banks should hold a substantial part of the war loan because it is exempt, for it is exempt in the case of any citizen as well as of the banks.

I was not objecting to it. It makes the loan easier, and more attractive. It might help the loan, certainly it

will not injure it at all. If my point has any influence at all, it should show that the loan is a better investment than it looked on the face of it, particularly to those who come under the clauses of the other tax bill. Exemption, as I figure it out, is practically equivalent to about 6i per cent under the ordinary circumstances; that is to say, if the individual were subject to the war tax. Exemption makes a difference of li per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not able to agree with my hon. friend. However, I do not think it is desirable that we should get into a mathematical argument.
Mr. LOGGIE-: Is there not a conflict in this section where it says that incorporated companies are to pay when they have a profit of over 7 per cent, and that persons are to pay when they have a profit of over 10 per cent? In the section, already passed, we have a definition that "person" means an incorporated company. The minister told us that "person" meant an incorporated company. If that is so, is there not a conflict between the two statements in this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend will read section 2 he will see that there is no conflict. The word "other" is there; it says "in the case of a business owned by any other person the rate of 10 per centum per annum upon the capital employed in such business."

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There has been a good deal of discussion upon the provisions contained, in this second section, but it seems to me that the point has never been made clear, at least not to me, why there should be a discrimination between incorporated companies and other persons. The incorporated company is allowed a profit of 7 per cent, and any other business is allowed a profit of 10 per cent. I repeat that the matteT has not been made clear to me why there -should be such a (difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In order to answer my hon. friend, it will be necessary for me to dwell for a moment upon the principle of -the Bill. The Bill is not a tax upon all profits, nor upon capital. The idea is this: Since the war broke out many persons, many firms, and many companies have not been able to maintain the rate of earnings which they maintained before the war. In many cases, net earnings have been
reduced, and dividends have been passed or reduced. In the case of other businesses, whether carried on by persons, firms, or companies, it is a fact that since the outbreak of the war net earnings have been maintained upons the pre-war basis, or even higher-In many industries and businesses of Canada very large net profits have been made. The principle of the Bill is this:	We fix
upon a rate of net profits which would be deemed reasonable in normal times and we say, in the case of -persons, firms, and companies which have, since the outbreak of the war, or in any accounting period ending since the outbreak of the war, not been able to make that percentage of net profit that they shall not pay because the' inference would be that they had suffered somewhat from the war... On the other hand, take the case of persons, firms and companies who have earned in the accounting period since the war broke out more than the norma] percentage of profit; the inference is in this case, speaking generally, that they would not be disadvantaged by the war. In many cases they have been greatly advantaged by the war, and the idea is to raise this taxation from these rather than from those of the former class. The idea is that those who have not been injuriously affected by the w-ar, and those who have made profits out of the war, should contribute a portion of those profits to the exchequer of the country for the purpose of carrying on the war; whereas, those who have not been able to maintain their normal rate of returns upon capital shall not be taxed. In answer, particularly to the question of my hon. friend; he does not understand why, in the case of private individuals and partnerships we allow 10 per cent on capital before the tax applies, whereas in the case of incorporated companies we allow 7 per cent only on capital before the tax applies. There are many reasons. The reason which appealed to me particularly when I brought down the Budget was that in the case of many companies-not all, but a large percentage-it is not possible to ascertain the precise cash value of the assets, as can be done in the case of firms and partnerships, because the matter has been complicated by the issue of stock for assets acquired by the company. That is one reason. Another reason is this:	An individual who
engages in business is responsible to the full extent of his estate for the debts of the business. In the case of joint stock companies shareholders enjoy the advantage of

limited liability. They can be called upon only to the extent of the shares for which they have subscribed or which they have paid up. Men are able to take an interest in many joint stock companies. Men, operating through boards of directors, are able to invest their capital in fifteen, twenty or more joint stock companies. They are liable in each one only to the limit of the shares which they hold in each, whereas, if a man goes into business for himself, or if partners engage in business, they are liable to the extent of their entire estates for the debts of the business.' It follows that an individual would expect, and would be justified in expecting, a higher rate of return in the case of a business conducted personally by himself without the benefit of limited liability. Men engaged in business for themselves, or partners engaging in business, expect to make, under ordinary business conditions, a return of at least 10 per cent upon their capital. I think that would be concurred in by business men. Let us take the case of joint stock companies, and particularly industrial companies which we are dealing with just now; seven per cent is the natural rate that occurs to one as representing a fair return upon the par value of stock paid up in a going concern. Preferred stock is usually put out on about a seven per cent basis. Men are willing, by reason of the advantage which they enjoy from the joint stock principle to take a less rate of interest upon their capital. They do not have to give the matter their individual attention, and they have the advantage of limited liability. These are some of the considerations which lead me to say that 10 per cent would be deemed, in a business community, only a reasonable return to a person, firm, or partnership, whereas seven per cent would be deemed to be a reasonable return upon .a business conducted by a joint stock company. In England, in applying this tax, their principle is the same. Taking a prewar standard, they fixed upon six per cent in the case of a limited liability company, and seven per cent in the case of persons, firms, and partnerships. But, so far as we can ascertain, having regard to the conditions of business, we think seven and ten per cent respectively would be a fair rate in this country.

I have never seen the English Finance Act, Bill No. 2, but I read the debate upon it when it was introduced by the Lord Chancellor. I understand that the profits taxed are the profits

which are in excess of the peace time profits. They, I understand, establish peace time profits by taking a period of three years, and they only tax the profits which are in excess of the peace time profits, but they tax them 50 per cent. I would like to know if I am correct in that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is in one respect correct in his conception of the Act, and incorrect in another. One principle of the Imperial Act was this: they established for a three-year period the net profits of a company which would become subject to the tax. They sought to establish the net earnings, or percentage of net earnings, for the three-year period. They made their legislation retroactive to the outbreak of the war, and they said to a company: If you have made more since the outbreak of the war than that average rate of profit, we are going to take 50 per cent of the excess.
That is what I say.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will understand that there are companies which had not been in existence three years previous to the war. Then they fell back upon this principle; they said: What prewar standard shall we fix upon? They fixed the pre-war standard at six per cent and seven per cent.
That was because they just had that profit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This six or seven per cent was what could be regarded as pre-war standard which would be fairly earned upon the capital of these companies. Section 40 of the British Act reads:
(1)	The profits arising from any trade or business to which this part of this Act applies shall be separately determined for the purposes of this part of this Act, but shall be so determined on the same principles as the profits and gains of the trade or business are or would be determined for the purpose of income tax, subject to the modifications set out in the first part of the fourth schedule to this Act, and to any other provisions of this Act.
(2)	The pre-war standard of profits for the purposes of this part of this Act shall, subject to the provisions of this Act be taken to be the amount of the profits arising from the trade or business on the average of any two of the three last pre-war trade years, to be selected by the taxpayer (in this part of this Act referred to as the profits standard) : Provided that if it is shown to the satisfaction of the Commissioners of Inland Revenue that that amount was less than the percentage standard as hereinafter defined, the pre-war standard of profits shall be taken to be the percentage standard.
The percentage standard shall, for the purposes of this part of this Act, be taken to be an amount equal to the statutory percentage on the capital of the trade or business as existing

at the end of the last pre-war trade year, subject. however, to the provisions of this Act as to any alteration in the manner of calculating the percentage standard in special cases.
The pre-war standard of profits was six per cent in the case of companies, and seven per cent in the case of individuals. The English Act is exceedingly complicated, and I desire to draw my hon. friend's attention to a feature in the English situation which does not exist here. My hon. friend knows there is an income tax in England, and that must be borne in mind when instituting any comparison between the English legislation and our own. All companies in England are subject to that income tax. In this country, of course, we have no income tax. If we institute a comparison in our legislation between the profits of a company in Canada since the war, and the profits of a company in Canada before the outbreak of war, in many cases some such result as this would occur:	A company might be earning twenty per cent before the war broke out. If it continued to earn twenty per cent after the war broke out, it would not pay anything. On the other hand, a company that was earning, let us say, six per cent before the war broke out might be earning ten per cent after the war. In that case, on the principle of the English Act, we should take half the difference between six and ten. It seems to me that it would be manifestly unfair to tax the company which is making only ten per cent and allow the other company which is making twenty per cent to escape. The principle of the English Act must be considered in the light of the fact that all those companies in England are subject to income taxation, which has been greatly increased since the outbreak of the war.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I have listened to the explanation of my hon. friend, but it seems to me that the distinction which he makes between incorporated companies and unincorporated companies is arbitrary and not at all fair. The rule is to be that an incorporated company will be allowed only seven per cent of profits before being taxed; but that an incorporated company, carrying on just the same kind of business, is to be allowed ten per cent. I have in mind in the city of Montreal two large retail dry goods stores. One I know is carried on by an incorporated company; as to the other I am not quite sure, but I believe it is unincorporated. These two stores stand side by side, are doing exactly
the same kind of business, running the same risks, and probably making the same rate of profit, but under these proposals one is to be allowed ten per cent, and the other only seven per cent. Now, it seems to me that this example shows very conclusively that the minister's method of selection has not been a happy one, and that an injustice will be done to some companies. It seems to me that the guiding principle ought to be, not whether a company is incorporated, or not, but the rate of profit it is making compared with other firms doing the same kind of business. What reason can there be for discriminating between two enterprises doing the same kind of business and making the same rate of profit, just because one is incorporated and the other is not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My right hon. friend has overlooked the point I madje with respect to limited liability. There is another point which I did not make, but which I desire to draw to his attention-as a general thing, in the case of partnerships comparatively small amounts are taken for administration, but in the case of joint stock companies, still speaking generally, the officials are paid, and the business is carried on by directors and other officers. It seems to me that the two points I have mentioned are of weight in this connection: first, the fact that in the case of many companies, if not most companies, there is a difficulty of ascertaining the precise value of the cash assets of the company; and, secondly, there is this feature of limited liability. As a result and consequence of that limited liability seven per cent is deemed to be a fair profit upon an industrial company, whereas ten per cent would, be looked for by a man who pledges his entire estate in the conduct of a private business. No doubt the figures have been fixed arbitrarily in one sense, and yet not arbitrarily in- another. In a tax bill you must fix arbitrarily on figures, and in reaching conclusions one should have regard to the general views of the community with respect to the matters dealt with. In the one case we have to consider what would be d,eemd -a fair return upon the capital stock of an industrial or busines-s company, and in the other what would be the percentage looked for by a private individual or partnership1 en-. gaged in business.

I agree with what the minister has said so far as limited liability

is concerned, but I can hardly agree that in a joint stock company more officers are required, and the administration expenses are greater. In many joint stock companies the stock is largely held by one person, the balance simply being held in a nominal way to comply with the Joint Stock Companies' Act. I do not think, therefore, that that argument would apply to any very great extent. However, that is not what I rose to take exception to. I have here a letter from a very large manufacturer in the western part of Ontario. I shall read a portion of it, not with the object of making any criticism, but for the purpose of getting information. My correspondent says:
It would seem to me that there ought to he a distinction made between financial companies and those engaged in manufacturing or business, but there should be no difference in the latter and the exemptions as between a company and partnership.
The instance that has been cited by the right hon. leader of the Opposition bears out the last part of my correspondent's letter, but it appears to me, although my view is subject to be corrected by the Minister of Finance, that so far as financial companies, pure and simple, and manufacturing companies are concerned, there ought to be some distinction made just ae is pointed out in this letter. I would therefore ask the Minister of Finance to say whether or not in his opinion there ought to be some such distinction made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would be difficult, under a measure such as this, to make any discrimination as between financial companies and other companies. After all, the proprietors of companies are the shareholders and the tax, of course, falls upon them. Now, shareholders of financial companies need their dividends just as much as do shareholders of industrial or other companies. I would say, that in the selling value of shares upon the market, in the case of a first-class financial institution, 6uch as a bank or loan company, the shares would sell upon a lower interest basis than in the case, let us say, of an industrial company. That is in accord with the argument of my hon. friend. '
Does my hon. friend not think that the risk in an industrial company is very much greater than that in a financial company?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
A good deal depends upon the industry; but, although

opinion has changed considerably in that regard in the last few years, owing to the specialization of our industries, generally speaking, I may say that industrial stock is regarded as somewhat more hazardous than the stock of a financial institution. My hon. friend, when he mentions purely financial companies, such as banks, trust companies, and loan companies, will recalls that, in my Budget speech of a year ago last February, we especially taxed those institutions; that is to say, we derive today out of existing taxation, apart altogether from this Budget, $1,000,000 from the banks, and a few hundred thousand dollars a year from the trust companies and loan companies. Resort was had to them in the first instance, and I think it could have been justified largely upon the idea that my hon. friend has in view. We now come to a point where we are imposing a more general and comprehensive tax. I have been unable, I am sorry to say, to see the question as between the joint stock company and the individual in the light in which my hon. friend from West Lamb-ton (Mr. Pardee) evidently regards it. I think there is a distinction between the two classes, and, in seeking to apply the principle of the measure, namely, to tax profits in excess of what may be regarded as a normal standard, I find it necessary to distinguish between the two classes of business and to give the advantage to the privately-owned company in which a private individual or a firm is responsible for the whole of the estate.
You will find small corporations, owned by the members of one family, who are conducting the business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The conduct of the business is practically the same as in the case of a partnership. My hon. friend, as a lawyer, will, I am sure, concede that in legislation it would not be
10 p.m. possible to discriminate as amongst joint stock companies.
I agree with my hon. friend that very often a family or a partnership turns its business into a joint stock company and then it becomes what is called a privately-owned joint stock company; but my hon. friend knows that next week those shares could be distributed and sold, and then the company would become what is known as a publicly-owned corporation. There is, 'however, no distinction in law between the two, and I do not see how it would be possible to discriminate by legislation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: You are going to start on a wrong principle.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not see how it is possible to discriminate between joint -stock companies, and to say that one is publicly-owned a,nd another is privately owned. A company, with the joint stock principle applied, is an entity different from all of its shareholders, and I do not see how we could discriminate.

Will land syndicates
come under this taxation measure? I have ' in mind several companies which, as my hon. friend knows, have cropped up in the good times under the late Administration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You mean just before the war?

For instance, a company has bought a strip of land, say in the suburbs of Montreal, and is incorporated, not to do business for all time to come, but just for the sale of that strip of land. Supposing it has partly sold the land, will it come under this taxation measure?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If a company has bought a tract of land and has sold part of it and is offering another part of it for sale, it is undoubtedly carrying on a business, and the question would arise under the provisions of this measure: What is its capital, its reserves, its accumulated profits? In other words, what is the amount of capital invested in that company and what are its net profits? No doubt in a case, such as my hon. friend has in view, there would be some difficulty in estimating the profits, but that is only a matter of administration under this measure; and, if it appeared upon a true balance sheet and a profit and loss account, that the company had earned for the accounting period a net profit in excess of 7 per cent, then it would come under this legislation.

The hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) raised quite an interesting point. There is no doubt that industrial companies are entitled to a greater profit than the trading concerns. Investments would not be made in industrial companies were there not a probability that very considerable net earnings could be made, for the reason, I suppose, that in prosperous years the profits must be abnormal in order to make up for the years in which substantial losses may be expected. Therefore, I think a distinction
might very well be made between industrial companies and trading concerns.
I d,id not, however, rise to discuss that matter, but rather to ask a question suggested by the remarks of the hon. member for West Lambton. Supposing a manufacturing concern in the year 1914 had been in business for ten years, and that for nine years it not only did not pay a dividend, but actually lost money, which had to be supplied by the company by borrowings or otherwise, and let us say that since the war began these manufacturers-say of leather-had been fortunate enough to make a great deal of money. In computing their liability under this taxation scheme, would the company in this case be allowed to deduct all additions to capital or back dividends before the minister could, step in and take his portion?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would say no. Here is a company which was earning practically no profits before the outbreak of the war, and by reason of the outbreak of war that company has been advantaged. We are Taising this money to help pay our expenditures in the war. We take from that company not all the earnings which it has made as a result of the outbreak of the war; we allow them first 7 per cent free, and then we say: if you make more than 7 per cent we take one-quarter of one per cent, so that if you make 15 per cent we take two per cent.
But that company may suffer losses for another period of five years after the close of the war. They may claim that they were entitled to excess profits.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think we could not have regard either to a period before the war or to a period after the war. The outstanding fact is that this particular company, in marked contradistinction to many businesses which have lost money as a result of the war, has made money as a result of the war. We say: if you have* made money as a result of the war, we are going to take a little of that money from you to help pay our share of the cost of carrying on the war.

The minister has said that one of the reasons that led him to place partnership companies on a basis of 10 per cent and incorporated companies on a basis of 7 per cent was the difficulty in getting at the exact cash value of the capital of incorporated companies. I must congratulate

the minister that on reconsideration he has vastly improved the resolution in that regard. As it was originally brought before the House, it certainly was not practicable, but as he has remodelled it, I think it meets the situation very well; it puts incorporated companies on practically the same basis as partnership companies. But the difficulty that led the minister to put partnership companies on a basis of 10 per cent and incorporated companies on a basis of 7 per cent has now disappeared, because he has found a way to get at the proper capital of over-capitalized as well as of undercapitalized incorporated companies. For the life of me, I cannot understand the equity of collecting from the partnership company one dollar and from the incorporated company four dollars. On a basis of 11 per cent earnings, you collect from the partnership company one dollar and from the incorporated company four dollars, or, in the larger number, $10, and $40, $100, and $400, $10,000 and $40,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
will permit me to correct him; I am sure that he does not desire to make an erroneous statement. My hon. friend has overlooked the fact that the Bill only takes one-quarter of the excess, so that if the percentage were 11, in the case of a firm, partnership or individual it would be one-quarter of a dollar, and in the case of a joint stock company, one per cent.

I quite understand that;
but what I say is absolutely true. If the minister will take a pencil and a piece of paper and work it out, he will find that on the basis of 11 per cent, for every dollar that the private company pays the incorporated party pays 'four dollars. On a IB per cent basis the proportion is as two to five; partnership companies pay two dollars while an incorporated company pays five dollars. On a 13 per cent basis, the partnership company pays $3 and the incorporated company $6. So that on the basis of earnings of 11 per cent, one company pays 400 per cent more into the treasury than the other company. Is that equitable? I have in mind in a certain district four or five unincorporated manufacturing concerns having a larger capital than $50,000, and right beside them are a number of incorporated companies. Can the minister give me any reason why there should be a spread on 11 per cent earnings of 400 per cent as between the amounts paid to the Crown by these different kinds of companies? The

minister has told us that in the United Kingdom there is a spread of one per cent, If the minister had suggested that the difference in this case should be one per cent, I should have been willing to consider it, but it does seem to me that the present proposal is unreasonable. The minister will find that the collection of this money will be attended with great difficulty; that the ' tax will be paid unwillingly by those who believe that the Government have not placed their company upon a reasonable basis as compared with that of other companies. I instanced a case in Ottawa and the minister has not replied. Can he tell me on what basis J. R. Booth of this city should escape paying any taxation, up to 10 per cent, whereas the E. B. Eddy Company and the W. C. Edwards Company will have to pay on their earnings over 7 per cent? I cannot see the equity of this, and I think that the minister will be well advised if he decreases the spread between 7 per cent and 10 per cent. If he makes it 7 per cent and 8 per cent there will be much less fault found with this measure when it comes to the collection of the tax. I would ask the minister to allow this to stand and to reconsider it. The right hon. leader of the Opposition instanced the cases of two dry goods firms side by side. Will the minister say why he should make it possible for one dry goods man to get his store rent free for three years? That is what it means, because the other man would have to pay the equivalent of his rent into the Crown, although he has the same earnings and stock. Many incorporated businesses are practically the same as though they were not incorporated. Of course in this I do not refer to the very large incorporated companies, such as the Canada Cement Company or the Canada Car Company. In such companies there is, perhaps, a significant difference, but in the ordinary incorporated companies, doing business say on the Miramichi river or in Bathurst or Shediac, the difference is very slight. I have in mind two businesses in Shediac that would probably come under the law, one incorporated and one conducted by a person. In the name of all that is fair and true, why should you ask one man to pay $4 and the other man to pay only $1, assuming the same basis of earnings and the same capital? My hon. friend has referred to the limited liability of the incorporated company and has advanced that as a reason why these companies are incorporated. I can give an-

other reason that is perhaps a greater incentive to incorporation, that is the question of succession; a business is incorporated so that in case of death the business can go on without interruption. Whatever advantage there is in that the companies pay for it when they get their incorporation papers. I think the minister is wrong in making a spread of 3 per cent, making the tax in some cases on one firm 400 per cent greater than on another.

Another reason for not having this inequality against the incorporated companies is that the company pays a provincial tax to the provincial treasury, whereas an individual or partnership does not. For the sake of argument and emphasis, take the case of our citizen, J. R. Booth. If his institution was incorporated at its proper value and his properties capitalized at anything near their actual value, and the business was conducted as a limited liability company, he would be paying many thousands of dollars in taxes to the provincial exchequer, through the provincial collector of revenue, whereas he * pays nothing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
So far as I am aware, there is always, in connection with public taxation, a discrimination against the joint stock company in favour of the individual, for the reason that the joint stock company does enjoy a privilege conferred by the State. This is simply a difference of opinion as to the amount of spread, and it seems to me it can best be determined by our considering again,what is the principle of the Bill. The principle of the Bill is to collect a certain amount of excess profit beyond what might be regarded as the normal percentage of return Supposing a private individual is going into business, he is going to pledge his whole estate in the business. If he fails, he loses everything. How large a percentage of return might he reasonably expect upon his capital? I ask the House to bear this further in mind, that in the case of individuals and firms no large salaries are taken out of the business as in the case of joint stock companies. A private individual gives his attention, day and night, to his business; he takes out in most cases only the amount of his living expenses; but in the case of a joint stock company they pay directors, they pay the president, they pay the officials, and they have to compete in engaging those officials with others requiring their services. All of these payments are taken out of the earnings before this tax. That raises a very strong consideration
in favour of the private individual as compared to the joint stock company in respect of the rate of return which may fairly be expected. Is there any man in this House who would go into general business to-morrow and give his time to it, day and night, taking out only his living expenses or a very small salary from the business, and accept a less return than 10 per cent upon his capital? ' That is question number one. Question number two is: In the case of a joint stock company, is it not a fact that the shareholders have the advantage of limited liability, that if the company fails they do not have to pay more than they have put in the company or subscribed upon its shares? Is there not a clear advantage there to the joint stock company which should be recognized in any legislation oi this kind? There is no province in this Dominion, so far as I know, there is hardly a state in the union, that does not impose taxation on joint stock companies because they are joint stock companies, because of the privilege they enjoy of limited liability, which is a much greater privilege than people generally recognize. Let us assume two businesses side by side. In one case, A, a private individual carries on business. He fails; he loses everything he has in the world. Beside him B, a more prudent man, who is worth a million of dollars says:	I am not going to risk my
million dollars. He will subscribe stock in a joint stock company to the extent of $200,000, and will engage in business alongside of A. B does not lose his million dollars; -he loses only $200,000.

Does the same difference in liability exist in Great Britain? What is the reason then for the difference in the spread as between 7 per cent and 10 per cent. Why should that spread be made so large in Canada when the spread in the liabilities as between [DOT] incorporated companies and private companies is so small?
$ir THOMAS WHITE: It does not necessarily follow that the British Act fixes the precise or correct standard in each case; that is open to argument. My hon. friend will hardly lay it down as a principle that we must be solely guided by British legislation. The point my hon. friend has overlooked is this:	interest rates are much
lower in England and there is a greater stability in an older country than in a new country and investors are, content with lower rates of interest. While I do not pretend to know the English situation, I

should assume that a private individual there would be more content with 7 per cent, having regard to the rate of return which can be obtained in the United Kingdom, than an individual in a comparatively new country like this, with no settled situation as they have in Great Britain. In this country they would expect 10 per cent.

I think that if the minister will examine the records, he will find that where men go into partnership concerns with a certain amount of capital- I do not mean men who go into business without capital, but men who go into business on their own account as partners with capital'-the percentage of failures is very much less than it is in the case of companies in which the same amount of capital has been invested in the first instance. In the case of partnerships a man handles his own money, but in the case of companies or corporations he has nothing to do with the control of the money, and in many cases the money is lost. The failures of corporations are very much more numerous than they are in partnerships where the same amount of money has 'been invested at the commencement of the business.

I am not interested in a private company, nor in a partnership; my interest, so far as manufacturing business is concerned, is all in joint stock companies. It strikes me that the spread of three per cent is fair. The advantage of a limited liability company is very great indeed. As every one knows, your assets, outside of your liability, in that company, are entirely free. Let me cite an instance which may bring more clearly before the committee the difference 'between a limited liability company and a private company or partnership. If there is a partnership, and you want to borrow from the bank say $10,000, $50,000, or $100,000, as the case may be, you go to the bank and endorse that note, and become responsible for it. In a limited, liability company you do not do that at all. If you were to ask the directors, or the stockholders, of a company to endorse the notes in a bank for the money borrowed to carry on the business they would absolutely refuse to do it.

I venture to say that 51 per cent of the corporations in Canada have their paper endorsed by their directors.
ISir Thomas White.]
' I quite agree that that is sometimes the case, but it is not always the case.
Pretty nearly.

I do not know of any company with which I am connected which has to do that; neither directors nor stockholders endorse individually. Surely the stockholders are never called upon to endorse; they are free entirely from that liability, whereas in a partnership, or in the case of an individual carrying on a business, he has to become responsible entirely for the money which he borrows, and for the capital which he invests. Not only that, his assets are liable as well. There is a very great difference, and although my interests are in stock companies, I think the spread is equitable and fair.

I want to present one idea to the minister. I presume that the object of this legislation is that it shall reach as many people who should be taxed as possible, and particularly those who have made profits on account of the war. It is pretty well known that there are a number of people in this country who are known as middlemen, and, who have made profits by getting contracts, and passing them over to others. I think the usual rate of commission is about 10 per cent in thefee cases. Under this legislation these people would, apparently, escape altogether. They have taken no business risks; they have, as a rule, provided no capital, and it seems to me that if there is any class of persons in the community who should be reached, it is that class. I have in mind some people who have done business on the percentage basis with the Government direct in purchasing war supplies, and who have received a commission of 10 per cent, and made considerable sums of money, with very little effort on their part, and, as I have stated, with no risk at all, and no capital. If these people escape, I think it would be most unfair.

If their profit is ten per cent, and does not exceed that, as individuals they would escape. If a company acted in that capacity, and made 10 per cent, they would not escape. I could mention names -they are well known. Take the Ellis Bros, of Toronto, for instance; they purchased binoculars for the Militia Department, and 10 per cent was the commission they received. I forget the total amount which they made, but it was quite a large sum

of money, and it was easily earned. Under the conditions that I have stated, if they were individuals, or were in private partnerships, they would escape.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I may point out, although I am not quite sure of the facts, that the firm of Ellis Bros, is an incorporated company, and any earnings that they may have made out of the transaction to which my hon. friend refers, would, I should think, be included in the company's earnings, and, consequently, they would become subject to the provisions of this Act. My hon. friend has spoken of middlemen. I inserted a provision in section 4 which I think will meet the case of individuals who have acted as middlemen and made large profits. Of course there will be cases of middlemen in petty transactions whom the Act will not reach, but if my hon. friend will look at subsection (a) of section
4.	he will see that the $50,000 limit does not apply to the business of any person who is or has been engaged in manufacturing, or in dealing with munitions of war. I put the words " or has dealings in " just to meet that case.
I have not the right resolution here then; there is no subsection 4.

The Minister of Finance is in rather an unfortunate position in regard to the resolution which he has introduced for the purpose of raising taxation. The principal reason for his taxation proposals apparently is that the minister has realized fully during the present session, and possibly before, that a large number of incorporated companies have made excessive profits out of the supply of munitions of war. I appreciate very much the attempt of the minister to get something out of the parties who have made such excessive profits, but while the minister, by the action he has taken, admits the propriety of the principle of attemptng to recover unjustly acquired profits, he finds himself in this unfortunate position that if he only levied thetaxupon those who have furnished munitions of war, he would be admitting the truth of what has been charged against the Government in this respect. To get clear of that dilemma, the hon. gentleman has seen fit to levy this taxation upon all corporations and partnerships doing business in the country. The tax that he is levying upon companies and partnerships for the purpose of obtaining the revenue that he requires is unfair and inequitable. My hon. friends have given illustrations of
the manner in which this tax will be applied. One cannot cite illustrations without being sectional, and without referring to matters that are personally known to himself. We have a number of incorporated companies in my county doing lousiness side by side with partnerships, and the inequality of the arrangement as applied to these two classes of businesses was well illustrated by my hon. friend from Northumberland (Mtr. Loggie). In my county there are two firms practically side by side carrying on exactly the same business. One business is carried on in the name of an incorporated company; it is purely and simply a family affair, an incorporated company having been formed by the brothers interested in the business. The neighbouring business is carried on under partnership, and if anything there is more money invested in the partnership than in the incorporated company. I happen to know these organizations, as I have done business with both. On what principle of equality is it proposed to tax the profits of the incorporated company exceeding 7 per cent while * the partnership can have a profit of 10 per cent without paying anything into the treasury? I do not know whether the minister has absolutely considered all the points raised by hon. gentlemen here to-day, or whether he has fully made up his mind to put this resolution through and levy the taxation on that basis, but I say that it is a most inequitable arrangement, and one which must raise a great deal of dissatisfaction throughout the country. I have had a number of letters and telegrams from my constituents protesting against this great inequality as between partnerships and companies. On behalf of these constituents I beg to draw the attention of the minister and the members of the committee to the matter. I sincerely trust that the minister will see his way clear to reconsider this proposal and put the different organizations which are being taxed on a more equitable basis so that they will pay an equal amount into the treasury whether they are doing business as incorporated companies or as partnership firms. The hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Lalor) speaking in regard to the status of companies as compared with that of partnerships, said that all the assets of the partnership are at stake. I may say to him that I know that the directors of a number of companies in my province, if they want to borrow .money from the bank,

have to go to the bank and endorse notes the same as private individuals have to do.
How about the stockholders; do they have to do that?
The directors own most of the stock.

It is not customary for stockholders to endorse notes, because a very large amount of the stock is generally held by the directors. One of the qualifications for a director is that he must hold so much stock. They usually go to the bank when they want to borrow money, sign notes as directors, and makes themselves personally liable. I know of some cases where the shareholders oi companies have also had to go to the bank with the directors and endorse notes to enable them to borrow money to carry on their business. I felt it my duty to bring these facts to the attention of the committee. They have come to me, not because I have any interest myself; I am in very few companies and in no partnerships. I am not speaking from the personal standpoint, but I am simply trying to voice the sentiments and complaints of a number of my constituents in regard to this matter. I would urge the Minister of Finance -to adopt some of the suggestions which have been made by hon. members on this side of the House.

I presume the minister will agree that one equitable way to have imposed this taxation would have been to have levied it on income. Might I ask him if he was influenced in any way against that plan by the suggestions of the provinces, or by an intuition that the provinces wished to retain that source of revenue for themselves? I have seen some discussion recently on that point. It is a well known fact that the provinces are having their difficulties, as well as the federal authorities, in finding new sources of revenue. In Ontario, for example, so long as we had our reserves of timber resources, these looked after the revenue fairly well.
At the present time the revenue is not coming from that source to any great extent. The provincial treasurer of necessity is looking for new sources of revenue. Some of,the incorporated companies that will be taxed under this Act have ben taxed for years by the provinces. A certain rate is also being imposed 'by the municipalities throughout the provinces for war purposes. I am inclined to think that the treasurer

of Ontario at least has his eyes on income taxation as a fruitful source of revenue at a not far distant date.
They will have to 6top dividend payments then.

The Minister of Finance seems quite shy of an income tax which would reach every person earning above a certain income. I think he had in mind that this source of revenue should be reserved to the provinces. Of course, the principle of direct taxation by the Dominion Government is comparatively new, and when the minister was considering possible sources of revenue he, perhaps, said: I will not impose taxation on incomes, but will leave that to the provinces. The remarks of my hon. friend from Haldimand (Mr. Lalor) are all right, but we are not all on velvet, as the saying is, and in as big a way as he is. War or no war, he goes along with an equanimity which a good many of us envy. But it was the smaller companies I had in mind, where the limited liability does not cut much figure. A large proportion of joint stock companies, at all events in Ontario, are formed for convenience sake. A father may want to get his two or three sons in the business, and as young men nowadays do not like to work with their father if there is nothing coming directly to them, a joint stock company is formed, and the stock distributed amongst the father and his sons.	But all of us are not fortunate enough to have sons, I am not referring to myself. On the one hand, then, we may have a father and his three sons engaged in a joint stock company, and on the other hand a man who has no family and is not in a joint stock company. He has only his capital. Now, the inequality comes in because one man is allowed to earn only seven per cent, while his neighbour is allowed to earn ten per cent. I am inclined to think that the spread is a little too great, particularly when we take into account the fact that a very large percentage of these businesses have been formed into joint stock companies, at all events in Ontario, merely for the sake of convenience and for the purpose I have outlined. The larger companies can look after themselves, but it does seem to me that it would be more equitable if some plan could be devised applicable to these smaller companies. In discussing this tax on business, I am not referring to those companies, whether large or small, that

have made big profits out of the war. We all agree that they ought to hand back a good deal of their profits, because we are all being heavily taxed on account of the war. But I am referring to the smaller companies that have been formed as family affairs, and which perhaps comprise seventy-five per cent of the whole. If the minister could include these companies in a separate class-it might not be easy to draw the line-I think it would remove a great many of the objections that some business men have to this legislation, and it would remove the feeling which some of them have that they are not being treated fairly as compared with others. A point was raised by an hon. member a few moments ago that has bothered me considerably. I am sure the Minister of Finance understands that I am not making these suggestions for the purpose of worrying him. Taxation, of course, is not welcome at any time, and we. are all of us interested in any taxation proposals. Under present conditions, however, taxation will be more cheerfully borne than under any other circumstances you could possibly imagine, and I want to assist the Minister of Finance so that every one will be satisfied that each is bearing his share of the taxation and no one more than his share. An hon. gentleman speaking a moment ago made this point, and it is particularly applicable perhaps to some of the smaller companies I have mentioned, and perhaps partnerships as well. Owing to the general revival in business on account of the war, many of these smaller companies not directly engaged in producing war supplies are in a much better position than they were a couple of years ago. Then they had their face, you might say, almost to the wall, but now many of them are sharing in the general business revival. Many of these companies may be using a portion of their surplus to pay off a heavy bank over-draft of a couple of years ago. Tliese companies will be taxed on all profits over seven percent, and I think when the war is over they are going to have a very, very difficult time. We all agree that it will be a miracle if there is not a decline in business in the readjustment period. After the war is over, this artificial business will disappear, and these smaller companies will have to look rto their ordinary business. Values are sure to go down, and I think many of these smaller companies will need a respectable part of their surplus to carry them over the readjustment period. I am afraid this taxation will have' the effect of driving some of these smaller companies out of business. I am not anxious about the larger ones; they are controlled by men of financial strength who can see their way to finance these companies as they go along. But I repeat that, unless you allow these smaller companies a fairly good reserve, many of them will go into bankruptcy after the war and they will blame it on this taxation. Of course, I know it is easy to make suggestions, but all my suggestions have been made in good faith and with a desire to get an equitable scheme of taxation. I think the minister and his experts might be able to devise some scheme whereby these smaller companies would be enabled to carry themselves through the readjustment period after the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I appreciate very much the admirable spirit in which my hon. friend has approached the consideration of this question. My hon. friend realizes that in any scheme of taxation that can be devised there will be anomalies when special cases are being dealt with. I had a very wide experience many years ago in connection with the Assessment Act of the province of Ontario, and I was struck particularly with the fact that from time to time special cases arose in which there appeared to be anomalies and even hardships, and yet it would appear impossible to draft a measure in which that does not occur.
I will now take up seriatim the points raised by my hon. friend. He speaks of this being a very heavy tax upon small companies. He will observe by the provisions of the Bill that it does not apply at all to companies unless the capital amounts to $50,000
That is a comparatively small amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-unless in the case of companies engaged in the manufacture of munitions, or in furnishing war supplies. I gave very careful consideration to the aspect of it that my hon. friend has very properly in mind, but the figures are not at all large. Take the case of a $50,000 company earning, let us say, 11 per cent. In that case the tax would be one per cent upon $50,000, or $500. Now, take the case of a company with $100,000 of unimpaired capital earning 11 per cent. The tax is only one per cent, or $1,000. A company

with a capital of $100,000, if it makes 11 per cent, is surely able, for the limited period of this measure, to contribute $1,000 towards the war. Take the .case of a company with an unimpaired capital of $1,000,000. If such a company made 11 per cent upon its capital it surely would not be a great hardship to ask it to contribute one per cent, or $10,000, towards the war. Therefore the amounts are not considerable.
Taking the comparison between joint stock companies and individuals, I have figures which I think will show that the spread, while it appears to be considerable, is, in realjty, not of very great consequence. Take the case of a company with a capital of $100,000 and earning, let us say, 20 per cent, or $20,000, in an accounting period. The tax which that company would pay would be one-quarter of $13,000, or $3,250 a year. Take the case of a partnership with precisely the same capital, $100,000, and earning precisely the same rate, namely, 20 per cent, or $20,000. The tax which that company would pay would be one-quarter of $10,000, which is the excess over 10 per cent, or $2,500. Subtract the $2,500 in the case of a partnership from the $3,250 in the case of a joint stock company and you get a difference of only $750 in the case of a $100,000 joint stock company and a $100,000 partnership, each earning 20 per cent. Having regard to the great advantage to the joint' stock company of limited liability, and to the other facts which have been adduced in argument here, I submit that $750 is not an unreasonable spread in the case of those two companies.
Needless to say, any Minister of Finance would like to avoid taxation; but it became apparent, not only to the Government, but to the Parliament and to the country, that in a time like this it is, to say the least, exceedingly desirable that we should pay as substantial a
11 p.m. part as we can of the principal of our war expenditure, especially when it is running into such large figures. And, further than that, as I have pointed out in previous discussions on the subject, I believe it to be indispensably necessary in the preservation of our country that we should show to the financial communities of the world that we are taking measures to meet the exceptional situation with which we are confronted, because it very much strengthens the hand of a minister and of a Government to be able, in issuing loans, to say to those who are to purchase the loans: The Dominion of Canada is facing the situation; it is im-

posing taxation; it is taking a part of the excess profits which have been earned on account of the war; it expects to raise a revenue of eight or ten or twelve million dollars per year from that taxation this year, and last year it imposed taxation which restored its revenue. Such action strengthens the hand of a minister and of a Government in selling its securities on the money markets of the world. This is a temporary measure, and the operative part of it comes to an end at the date mentioned in the Bill, that is to say, the 31st day of December, 1917. It is true that in the succeeding year there will be a payment in respect of the accounting period falling due during the year 1917, but the Bill is designed to last only three years, and it will not last longer than that.
Did not my hon. friend, when he was introducing this Bill, say that we might expect some further taxation later on?

It would depend somewhat upon the rate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should point out that the provinces and municipalities do, for the most part, although there are some exceptions, levy an income tax. That is to say, the municipalities in some provinces levy an income tax under provincial authority for municipal purposes. In one of the provinces, or in some of them, the province itself levies a direct income tax. My hon. friend may be on sound ground in stating that the tendency will be for the provinces to resort more and more to income tax. Without pronouncing at all upon the policy of the Dominion Government with regard to the matter of income taxation-because it is not really before us at the present moment-there are some considerations that I should, like to mention. I have given a good deal of thought to the question, not only in connection with Budget, but since I became minister I have reflected a good deal on modes of taxation. It must be borne in mind that this country is one of large area. It is as large as the continent of Europe; it is larger than the United States. As we have a sparse population in the administration of an income tax by the Dominion very heavy cost in proportion to the amount realized would be involved as compared with the cost of administration in the United States, where it is admittedly very high. It is, I think, a sound maxim or canon of taxation that, in considering a tax, regard should be had to the cost of collection. If the cost of collection is very high, it is a sound maxim of taxation that that form of taxation has an objectionable feature. Of course, the object of taxation is to get money for public needs, and if in the collection of money for public needs a very large percentage is necessarily absorbed by collection, the result is that the tax to that extent is imposed for the benefit of the collectors. I submit these considerations because I was much impressed by the speech of the hon. member for Halifax, in which he said that the time would come when a comprehensive system of taxation might be necessary in this country. I am throwing out these observations as showing some of the considerations that would, have to be taken under review in considering the question of an income tax by the Dominion Government. I have adverted to the matter Thomas White.]
ter of cost, and at this time it would seem to me particularly inexpedient for the Dominion to embark on income taxation. An army of officials would be required in a country like Canada, because the woTk would, have to be done thoroughly or should not be done at all. We should have to establish almost a new Civil Service. I do not desire to exaggerate the magnitude of the service, but it would be very large. We should have to have assessors and their clerks in practically every township, every county, every village, every town, and every city, for the purpose of levying the assessment; afterwards we should have to have machinery for revision and collection. I need not say that that would be a formidable undertaking.
These are some of the considerations which are involved in the question of an income tax. I do not consider it necessary to express any opinion as to whether or not in the future the Dominion would at any time resort to such a tax. I think it would be most inexpedient for me to pronounce any opinion upon that. My hon. friend referred to some smaller privately owned companies. I think that as a legislator of experience he will realize that even though there is some anomaly and some hardship -if such a term may be implied to a Bill which imposes such a moderate measure of taxation unless in case of excessive profits -there would be great difficulty in discriminating between joint stock companies. After all, a joint stock company is a joint stock company, and I do not see how we could treat one joint stock company differently from another. I think I have dealt with nearly all the points raised by my hon. friend from Renfrew (Mr. Graham), and I take the opportunity of again expressing my appreciation of the very fair view he has taken of this measure and his realization that there is room for difference of opinion.

I think the principle of
this taxation is all wrong. In my judgment it is imposing a penalty on thrift.
Hear, hear.

For instance, take a corporation or company who use judgment, energy and ambition, and handle their business economically, wisely and prudently, they are punished for doing so. I think it is a bad principle; it is against progress. Furthermore, I think you will find it will have a tendency to drive capital from this country that would otherwise come in and

invest. Immediately they realize that their ' capital will r*, taxed 25 per cent of their earnings, they will steer clear of it. I know of one or two firms that were seriously considering erecting plants in Quebec who are now hesitating. They say: This is the beginning of it and we do not know what the end will be. I think that will apply all over the country. The principle itself is wrong, and without any reflection whatever on the Minister of Finance, who comes to this House with a reputation as a clearheaded, clever financier, I think if he had used his own best judgment in working out a system of taxation, if he had not, perhaps, listened to the Minister of Elections, he would have succeeded better than he has done.
Mr. LAiL/OR: I think it is the minister who is hit.
Mr. MoOREA: He is perhaps willing to he hit. The Minister of Finance will find that the tax will not touch fifty per cent of the people who are well able to-oontribu-ture their share of taxation, and who are willing to contribute. This Government are, I think, the most fortunate Government that ever held office in Canada, so far as taxation is concerned-remember, that is as far as I wish to go. Taxation of any kind is never welcome. It is never very much appreciated by the people of Canada. But at this particular time, 1 think the people of Canada realize that taxes have to be imposed, that they have got to pay taxes, and they are willing to pay them; but, they want to be taxed equally; they want this burden to be distributed so that it will bear equally and fairly on all parties. If that is done, I think there will be no complaint or grumbling about it. It is perhaps easier to make criticisms of this kind than to devise a scheme for obtaining that object. Nevertheless, it is, in my judgment, true that this taxation will not touch fifty per cent of the people who are willing and well able to pay their share of th'e burdens that have to -be borne. I am glad it is only a temporary arrangement. I hope that our Finance Minister will not forget that, and that it will be done away with very soon.

speechtext: I am on record.
