speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The matter of administration, of which my hon. friend has referred, might, I think, be more conveniently taken up when we reach section 11, which deals with that phase of the taxation. I shall be very glad indeed to deal with it then, if that will be acceptable to my hon. friend.

When I was addressing the committee, the Finance Minister took issue with me as to the rate of taxation on an
II	per cent basis. Does he admit that I was correct in my statement that one company would pay $4 while the other company would pay only $1?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I did not quite follow my hon. friend. I have no desire to challenge his figures, except to say that I think if he will take an example say of the case of a one hundred thousand dollar company and a one hundred thousand dollar firm, and assume that they make 11 per cent or 15 per cent, and then work out the actual result under the Act, he will find that the difference is comparatively small.

I have that actually
worked out, and I wish to tell the minister and prove to him that what I say is absolutely true. The earnings of $100,000 at 11 per cent are $11,000. In the case of a partnership, there is 1 per cent over. One per cent of $100,000 is $1,000, and 25 per cent of that is $250. In the case of an incorporated company, $100,000 at 11 per cent iS $11,000. There is 4 per cent over. On $100,000 that amounts to $4,000. Then 25 per cent of that is $1,000. Thus, in the

case of the incorporated company, the tax will be $1,000, and in the case of the' partnership company the tax wdll be $250, so that the incorporated company pays $4 for $1 that the partnership company pays.
I	do not think that the illustration the minister gave us was a fair one. He gave the illustration of earnings 20 per cent. That is a most uncommon rate; it is uncommon in the Maritime Provinces to earn even 11 per cent. If we do that we consider ourselves mighty lucky. It is no use to bring up an illustration of 20 per cent. When the percentage is less than 11, a company would pay $750 and the partnership would pay nothing. If they earn 9 per cent, the tax would still be very heavy in the one case as compared with that imposed on the other; I think it would be $500 against nothing. If they earned 1 per cent less, that would mean $250. against nothing paid by the partnership. On the basis of
II	per cent, a company would pay $4 for every $1 that the individual or partnership would pay.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is a good mathematician, but I am afraid he has not considered how little that really means. He is dealing with a company that has $100,000 of capital, and with an individual or firm or partnership that has $100,000 of capital. That is a fairly substantial capital, but in the case he has given, there would be a difference of only $750. A company with $100,000 capital pays only $750 in the case he has instanced more than the individual or partnership. That is only $7.50 per $1,000 of capital. That is all that this tax penalises, so to speak, a joint stock company with its privilege of limited liability as compared with an individual or firm or partnership. I do not think that that is a very serious matter at a time like this in a tax which, as I have stated, is for a limited period.

The minister tries to get away from the point by saying that the amount is not very large. That is not the question at issue. The question is, why should there be a spread of 3 per cent. Suppose the capital is $500,000; then the payment by an incorporated company will be $5,000, as compared with $1,250 in the case of a partnership. In three years that would amount to $15,000, &s against $3,750, an amount sufficient to buy a store in a town of 5,000 or 6,000 inhabitants.

I am almost beginning to feel that I am on the wrong side of the

-House. The champions of the manufacturers and joint stock companies are our friends opposite. My experience in the House, spread over a good many years, does not bear that out. I find my hon. friend from Sherbrqoke (Mr. MoCrea) taking the view that the manufacturers and joint stock companies are taxed too heavily. I agree that they are taxed pretty heavily. Then there is my hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. Loggie) I am quite surprised to hear him take up the attitude he has adopted to-night, because he has always taken the ground that the manufacturers and the joint stock companies were the people who were extorting too much m,oney from the people, in fact, practically robbing them. I should have thought that he would have welcomed the taxing of these companies. It is quite encouraging to find hon. gentlemen opposite taking up this new position. The first thing we know will be that they will say there is not enough protection, and that there should be more. There is one thing that strikes me in .connection with this Bill. It seems to me that in place of the limit being fxed at $50,000 it should be $40,000. In the province of Ontario a tax is imposed on joint stock companies with a capital of over $40,000, and the result is that a great many companies are incorporated, with a capital of $40,000. I think that very few are incorporated with a capital of $50,000.
It is the same way in other provinces; the limit is $50,000, and many of them are incorporated with a capital of $49,000.
The companies incorporated with a capital of $40,000 might escape altogether.	.	.

In so far as I understand taxation, there are only three methods that can be adopted. One is to tax expenditure, the second property, and the third income. If I remember Tightly, the Minister of Finance, in his Budget speech of last year, made a raise alt through the tariff, and it was bitterly attacked by hon. gentlemen opposite. Certainly that was a tax on ex-, penditure, because the money raised is on the expenditure of the people, on their imports into this country. The second method' of taxation is to tax property. That is a form of taxation which was adopted^ by the province of Ontario last year in levying a rate of one mill on the dollar on property in the province. I remember the drastic eriticism to which the Ontario Government

[DOT] 1861
was subjected. The critics said that it was not fair, because the assessment throughout the province was not equal, that the assessment in the cities was higher in relation to value than the assessment in the counties, and that if the Government wanted to adopt such a system of taxation they should: equalize the assessments, equalize land values and business taxes throughout the province. Hon. members understand how great a work that would be. Then we come to the Finance Minister's proposition this year. Certainly it is an income tax, but it is an income tax on ithose who are able to pay, upon the men who have made money, directly or indirectly, through this war. In my judgment, it will commend itself to the people of this country, as it certainly commends itself to me. If I believe in taxation at all, and we must believe in taxation, the man who can pay is the man who should pay at a time like this. I believe that it is the man who is wealthy who should contribute to the maintenance of this war, and I am certain that that is the sentiment of the people at large. I am not going to express any opinion as to whether or not it might be necessary ultimately to establish an income tax on a Dominion basis. Perhaps that time may come, and if it does come, I hope the Minister of Finance will consider carefully the entire scheme, because an income tax is not the simple thing that some people would have us believe. You have to take into consideration the difference in the tax paying power of single men as compared with married men; the capacity of the man with a family to pay as compared with the capacity of the man who has no family, and the question of how great an exemption should be given to the man in the city as compared with the man in the country. All these things cannot be worked out in a minute. I think the Minister of Finance has met the opinion of the country at large in bringing down his measure of taxation, and if it should be necessary at a future time to bring down an income tax, I am satisfied that the people have confidence that he will bring down a well-devised scheme.

I have a word to say by way of suggestion. I think there should be some limit in the case of a partnership. II

the capital invested in a partnership reaches a certain limit the partnership should be put upon the same basis as a corporation. The biggest industry you have in the city is owned by one individual. Is it fair that that industry should be allowed 10 per cent profit on its capital before being taxed as against some of its neighbours, who are probably a good deal harder up and have a smaller investment?
